utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. We thought, Counsel Radovic, if you don't mind, to put off a discussion of this matter of provisional release until the end of the coffee break, so as not to interrupt the flow of cross-examination by Counsel Krajina, which -- I think probably it's better. Counsel Krajina intends to finish by 10.30. Then we will have a coffee break, and then after that we will move to this particular item. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I should like us now to go back to the testimony of some witnesses before this Court. Witness B, who testified on the 24th of August, 1998, said about you, Mr. Kupreskic, that on the 15th of April 1993, he saw you in front of the Hotel Vitez, where the HVO headquarters were at the time. Do you remember this testimony?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the testimony very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Right. So will you please tell us if you think that this witness told the truth, and if not, why not.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What Witness B said is absolutely not true. To begin with, because at that time, on the 15th of April 1993, I was not less than 100 kilometres away from that particular place. Secondly, the manner in which Witness B described it, that he saw me from his car as he was driving -- that is, through glass, at a certain speed, from a distance not less than 30 metres, with all sorts of obstacles between us, I think all brings the statement into question. However, I never came to that hotel, I never came to that HVO headquarters. I had no need to go there, and I never, ever, went into the part of the hotel where the headquarters was. Secondly, I remember well Witness B and an officer, I think a reconnaissance officer. And if that is all he told this Court about me, then I can be quite happy with what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Will you please tell us, did you know Witness B well? Did you use to socialise at some time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (redacted), but we have not met for the past 15 or 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because he went very early to schooling in Belgrade, and there he completed his schooling, and after that he went to work in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: What school did he go to? What was he?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He graduated from the military academy, and he worked for the Yugoslav People's Army as an officer, and he came home very seldom, that is, once every couple of years. So I can really say with certainty that we have not met for at least 15 years, particularly during that period of time when people's physical appearance changes, both his and mine. All this shows that he could not see me there, and I was not there at the time, besides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Enough about that. A witness with the pseudonym "G" testified on the 1st of September 1998 and said that he had seen you several days after the 16th of April 1993, going around some deserted houses in Ahmici, and the witness described it as if you were there in order to steal something, or something like that. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember that testimony of Witness G. It is a boy who was only 13 years old at the time. At that time, I was not there, because one could simply come near the village. At the time, I was in Donja Rovna. But if we recall the testimony of that witness, that witness was for some seven or eight days in a very serious predicament, without food, without water, in that house, and he was often unconscious during that time. If you also remember that through the window of that particular house, that this is 300 metres, that he saw my back, that he saw me from the back, these circumstances indicate that this is not possible. Moreover, if I may add about Witness G, that boy came to my house -- I believe it was 1996 or 1997; I can find out exactly when -- and I never knew about his suffering, and he came to ask me to buy his land. I refused it, and I only gave some presents for him and his sister. That was the end of our conversation. However, some time later, Witness G came again, found me and asked for a couple of thousand marks from me. He said he needed money to go to another country. I did not do that, and probably, and as you heard here, because of that -- and he also said that he wanted political asylum. So his false testimony must have been due to those reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. A witness, and she appeared here as Witness H, testified here on September 1998, and she said that on the 16th of April 1993, around 6.00 in the morning, she saw you pass through her yard in which her father was killed that day. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: To begin with, let me tell you that at 6.00 on that day I was not there. I was in Jozo Vrebac's shelter, that is, I was about 2 kilometres away from that place. But I do remember the testimony of that girl well, of Witness H. I watched her with great attention, and I can say, really, that she testified out of fury, that is, out of revenge because she had lost her father, and the only father is the real father, and she lost him. I really wonder, how is it that Witness H did not also place me within the context of those events in the house together with my cousins. Presumably she knew that she had never seen me either with a weapon or in a uniform, and she wanted to show that I had run by at the time, at that moment. To a degree, I can understand, and I can perhaps -- it is very difficult to face such a situation. Perhaps my daughter would have testified in a similar way had it happened to her, had she lost her father, and they are about the same age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: This girl, this witness, also said that she talked to you after the war, that in a conversation, you questioned her right to come to Ahmici. Do you remember that part of testimony, and is that true?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that is not true. The circumstances are somewhat peculiar. At that particular time, when she came for a couple of minutes, I would happen to be there and accept the conversation with that witness, with a child. The way she described that meeting, she was in a car with three more persons sitting in the back, she had broken her leg, and with the sound of the engine, she talked to me, who was 30 metres away from her, that she communicated in that manner, that is very illogical. Besides, to discuss such matters with a girl, with a little girl, I really see no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Witness [redacted] testified on the 4th of September, 1998 and, in his testimony, said that on the 16th of April, 1993 in the morning, he saw you in a blue coat, that you passed through the yard in front of the house of his slain son. What can you tell us about that? You also will remember that he said he watched it from the window of his house.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember [redacted] [redacted]. That is not true. At that time, I was in the shelter and he could not see me. Besides, I don't know about a blue coat because I never had a blue coat. But if I may, Mr. President, Your Honours, I should like to use a small sketch in order to explain the statements of that witness where he shows two different places in which he saw me that morning and the discrepancies between his testimony and his

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: [redacted]. It will be very brief, just to make things quite clear. Thank you very much. I shall begin by explaining the sketch and the captions so that we can all follow this. So these red marks are me at places where [redacted] saw me. This here is the south side, so this is the main road to Gornji Ahmici. This is the warehouse. Next to my warehouse, this is my house. This is Sukrija Ahmic's house and his son, this is his stable, and this is Sakib Ahmic's house. This window marked "Z" is that west window which means that this is west and, of course, opposite to it is east, north, south. I shall only read the [redacted]

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: [redacted]. "When the attackers left --" it shall be very short really, "I went back to the bedroom," so that is this marked with Z, facing southwest. It's here, like this. "I saw four or five HVO men in the yard of this -- in Vlatko Kupreskic's house." It is here. "The HVO men were about 50 metres away," so this is here, 50 metres, "from the window at which I was standing. The day was just breaking. It was a nice and clear day. At about the same time when I saw those HVO men, I also saw Vlatko to the right of me," which confirms that he, indeed, saw me in this part. "He was wearing civilian clothes and was moving towards his house. When he reached his house, he went on, and he passed by HVO men, turned around their house to the right, and I could not see him again." I shall merely remind you of the [redacted]

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: [redacted] says that he saw me here, that is, between his son's house and my own house. That is at a completely different place, not to the southwest but to the southeast, and only in order to make the testimony of Witness H more veracious. But I was passing through, and here I ran through. Thank you very much. That's as far as [redacted] [redacted] statement is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness with the pseudonym "L," who testified on the 17th of September, 1998, said that on the 15th of April, 1993, you were with a group of soldiers in front of your shop in Ahmici and that the soldiers were in your warehouse and on your balcony, on the balcony of your house, that is, on the 15th of April. Will you please comment on this? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not true. On the 15th of April, 1993, at that time indicated by Witness L, I was, for all intents and purposes, in a different state. I was not there. We can all recall Witness L, and, of course, that is my next-door neighbour. All I can say is that he is mentally unaccountable, that he's prone to drinking, and I also know that his nervous system was damaged because he went to bathe in the Lasva River sweaty and all hot, and ever since that time, he does not have -- he lost self-control. I can remind you also of his testimony here. He says: "Around 4.00 in the afternoon, I had a beer in Vlatko's house. Ivica and Vlatko were sitting at a table in front of the house, and Mirko Vidovic was sitting there with them. And as I was sitting there, I saw soldiers in Vlatko's house." But, you see, to begin with, all three of us were in another state. Mirko Vidovic was in Germany; Ivica and I were in Croatia. But now look, from this testimony, he says that on the 15th of April, he saw us in front of my house at a table, whereas Witness L says that those soldiers were sitting in the house. Now, can you imagine the circus? They were sitting in the house and the three of us were sitting at a table drinking beer. Then in his testimony here before the Court, which Witness L gave on the 17th of September, 1998, he moves me and all three of us to a completely different place. He places us now in front of my shop where the three of us were sitting and drinking beer but without him. Two completely different statements. But that witness, as I have said, is mentally sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us proceed. Witnesses M and O mention in their testimonies before the Court that in the night between the 15th and the 16th of April, 1993, they saw lights in your house and that looked strange to them. Will you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As for the testimony of those two witnesses, they are saying the truth because the lights were on all the time at my balconies. Invariably on the first floor, that was the case before the war, during the war, and practically until the present day. In front of my house and in the parking space, I keep my vehicles parked. In order to have proper safety, the lights were on all the time. On this first balcony outside, both light bulbs were turned on all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness T testified on the 24th of September, 1998 and she said that she saw you carrying some weapons from your car into your house in the autumn of 1992. Is that correct, what this witness said, and what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never carried any weapons. I said that I obtained a rifle only after the war, that is to say, in January 1995. That is certainly incorrect. Of course, many times, I unloaded merchandise I had because I had merchandise in the house, and I would carry it from the car to the house; however, these were smaller parcels and these were expensive goods. All the other goods were unloaded by my workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Finally, I'm just going to refer you to another witness's statement. Witness Q, in his testimony of the 23rd of September, 1998, says that he recognised you as you stood in a group of soldiers that was shooting in front of your house and killed his wife on the 16th of April, 1993 in Ahmici. Please, what can you say about the truthfulness of this statement?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is incorrect. First of all, do you remember this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I remember this statement.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not correct. At that time, I was not there at all. I said where I was. The first time I managed to get to my house was at 13.00, and that is when I found the soldiers, but in my house. After that, I managed to come back to the house only around 6.00. So this is absolutely incorrect. I was not there at the time and I was not with the soldiers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation? Do you have an opinion concerning this? Why would this witness incriminate you in such a way?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, of course, I wondered an innumerable number of times why this is so, why this man is incriminating me and how he could have done this to me. I have an explanation which may be logical, namely, the following: That morning, a war had broken out, and there was shooting all over. People were shooting at his house and soldiers had done that. And, of course, he could not recognise anyone. He lost his wife. His daughter was wounded. He wanted to blame someone. Who could he have blamed but me, his next-door neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: And why you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably because he thought that the shooting was coming from my house and from in front of my house, and then he probably said, "It is the Croat's fault, as far as I'm concerned. It is Vlatko's fault, as far as I'm concerned. Let him go to court. Let him try to justify himself there. If he is not guilty, let him say who is guilty." You could have noticed here that quite a few witnesses asked me to say who did it. But allow me to draw a different comparison. Let me be realistic. Had, heaven forbid, my wife been killed on that morning and had shooting come from Witness Q's house or from around his house, it is hard to say, but I believe that I would incriminate him too, I would accuse him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I have no other witness statements that I would like to show you. But, Mr. Kupreskic, in your testimony so far, we have referred to the indictment and the evidence on which the indictment against you is based. During your witness statement, you denied all these counts in the indictment and all this evidence. You are claiming that all of this is untrue; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing, none of that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Please, do you have an explanation then how come and why were you indicted? Why were you indicted, although you did not take part in any of this? Can you say something about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Through my testimony, I have responded to this question to a large extent, but perhaps I should round this off now. I believe that the only reason is my house, it is my house that is to be blamed, my house that was in that particular spot. The soldiers who violently entered it, who broke down the door and who were shooting from that house and from in front of that house, and where, indeed, my innocent neighbours were killed and wounded, they could not recognise anyone, when I did not recognise these men when I was practically facing them. So naturally, they accused me, as their next-door neighbour. The exclusive reason, therefore, is my house. I could not in any way influence these soldiers or prevent them from doing something. You heard Colonel Watters, who was a witness for the Prosecution. He is a military man, and he says that he could not oppose this military and the objective that they wanted to achieve, so how could I do that? So the thing that is to be blamed is my house only, and the fact that I'm their next-door neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. Now I would like to ask you the following: Today, when you view all these tragic events from the vantage point of the present day, do you see any mistake that you made at the time, Mr. Kupreskic? Would you have perhaps acted differently today than you did in those moments?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I really did not do anything wrong. I've been thinking about this until the present day. What could I have done that would have been better and smarter than what I did during those days and before the war and on that day itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Very well. And, finally, could you please tell us whether you feel responsible and guilty in any sense, criminal or moral, with regard to your behaviour during this incriminated (sic) time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I absolutely do not feel guilty. Not morally, and least of all, criminally. I did not kill anyone. I did not do any evil to anyone. I did not torch anyone's house. I did not harm anyone. Until that 16th of April, 1993, not through a single thing I did in the village, because I did not carry weapons, ever, or did I wear a uniform, or did I attend a single meeting. I never hoisted a flag on my shop. Not through a single gesture did I contribute to any provocations against my Muslim neighbours or these events, these war events of the 16th of April, 1993. What could I have done? Had I known what would have happened, the only thing that I could have done that would have been smart was to have left, to have gone to another state, escaped. It is only in that way that perhaps I would not find myself here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have concluded my questioning. I tried to use as little time as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Counsel Krajina, for being, as usual, concise and to the point. We may now, probably before we move on to cross-examination, probably we could discuss the matter of provisional release, if Counsel Radovic is agreeable. Counsel Radovic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: My colleagues rightly suggest to me that probably the witness should go back to his seat over there. When we resume, then, you will again take the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of Zoran Kupreskic, and on behalf of my colleague Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, on behalf of Mirjan Kupreskic, I am submitting a motion to apply Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which speaks of the possibility of provisional release of accused persons. According to this Rule, the Trial Chamber can order provisional release only under exceptional circumstances. What are exceptional circumstances? That is not regulated by legal regulations. It is up to the Trial Chamber itself to judge whether the circumstances that are mentioned by the accused in favour of his provisional release belong to the category of exceptional circumstances. Yesterday, in my introductory remarks, I mentioned a motive for submitting this motion, so one of the motives was the visit of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal to the Republic of Croatia and her talk with the Croatian Minister of Justice. A subject was raised, inter alia, in that talk that certain accused could be provisionally released -- at least, this is according to what the press reports in the Croatian press said -- that the Prosecutor did not reject that proposal, but it had to be presented, such proposals had to be presented to the Court on a case-by-case basis, and then the circumstances would be looked into. The Defence of Mirjan Kupreskic and of Zoran Kupreskic believe that there are exceptional circumstances in this respect, and that they are twofold. It is not only the fact that the summer is beginning, and it is hot in our part of the world and it is windy here, and that the trial has been going on for a long time, but also the entire situation has to be viewed, that is to say, the situation in which some of the accused find themselves, and especially their family circumstances have to be taken into consideration. With regard to the two Kupreskics -- that is to say, Zoran and Mirjan -- a major problem is their mother, Luca, who was born in 1937, who lives on her own in the house that belonged to their late father, and who is very ill. She has trouble with her pituitary gland, and on two occasions she underwent surgery. She takes medication for her pituitary gland and for blood pressure every day, and she is supposed to go for medical treatment, but she hasn't been for medical treatment for a year because the appropriate medical equipment does not exist in Vitez, but this equipment only exists in Mostar. Since she has only minimal revenues, she is not in a position to leave Vitez and go anywhere. She is fortunate to make do with the little money she receives. It is a generally known fact that psychological stress affects a person's blood pressure and pituitary gland, and she is in constant stress on the basis of the fact that Mirjan pointed out yesterday, and that is to say that she is probably the only mother in the world that has two sons who are indicted for war crimes. Therefore, both sons are very afraid for her life, and they think that her medical condition would considerably improve if they were to go home, at least on a temporary basis, until a final ruling is made. As regards Zoran Kupreskic, his wife, Mira Kupreskic, was born in 1963. One month after the accused voluntarily surrendered to The Hague, she also had trouble with her pituitary gland, and two or three months later, she had ovarian tumours detected, but surgery could not be carried out immediately because first the pituitary gland had to be treated. So surgery was carried out only in October 1998 in Zagreb, and that is when she had a hysterectomy performed and her ovaries were removed too. She has to go for medical checkups every month, and, as of late, it has been once every two months, and at that time her three children remain alone at home without appropriate parental guidance. Zoran Kupreskic has problems with his children too. He has three children: Mladen, born in '85; Anto, born in '92; and Davor, born in '89. For a month, these children, Mladen and Anto, have bronchitis, which has been going on for the past three years. Their medication has to be paid for every month, and it is recommended that at least once a year, they change the climate they live in for a month, that is to say, that they should go to the seaside. His wife cannot do that, not only for financial reasons, but also because this is medically not recommended to her, that is to say, the wife is prohibited from doing the kind of things that are recommended for the children's treatment. Their son Mladen, who was very close to his father, is now entering adolescence, and his mother cannot exercise sufficient control over him in order to stop the various trouble that he has been making as an adolescent. During the war and after the war, Vitez is not a town where people are no longer inclined -- it is not a town where there is not exactly a vice problem, so she is afraid that her son will get in touch with drugs. The father therefore believes that it is essential that he should be there and prevent the possibility of a drug problem. As for Mirjan Kupreskic -- the same goes for Zoran Kupreskic, as well -- his wife is unemployed, and he has two children. The son, Marko, who was born in 1991, has certain psychological problems, and he goes to see a psychologist every day. His problems are such that he is the only child in the area of Vitez who did not manage to finish the first grade of elementary school, and now he will have to attend a special school. Also, it is quite uncertain how, under the present circumstances, given his father's absence, he will manage to succeed in doing this. The daughter, Marija, who was born in 1998, after the father came here, has psychological problems. She has a stammer, that is to say, she has speech problems, and she would have to undergo therapy in that respect. In the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, the only efficient treatment for this -- that is to a say, to deal with these speech problems and the stammer itself -- this can be resolved only at an institution which is called Suvag, which is within the University of Zagreb, the faculty of philosophy. Both of his children are traumatised by war, and now, after the war, they have taken this very hard, that is to say, their father's absence. Both children also have eye problems, and they wear glasses. These are the general conditions. As for the conditions here, with all the good will of the Trial Chamber to speed up the proceedings, objectively speaking, the proceedings have been going on for quite some time. The accused came here voluntarily. That is not to say that anyone arrested them; it is through their own free will that they came here. During their stay in prison, or that is to say in prison circumstances, they have behaved in an exemplary fashion. This can be checked with the detention unit authorities. We think that the first, the second, and the third matters could be categorised as exceptional circumstances for provisional release. In addition to this, we would like to say that the accused, before coming to The Hague voluntarily, tried to establish contact with the Office of the Prosecutor here in The Hague, and they wrote various letters, including a letter to the president of this Tribunal. At the time when these letters were written, the president of this Court was the president of the current Trial Chamber. If you allow them to go back home to the territory of Vitez, they are prepared to observe all the terms and conditions that you would impose upon them and that are envisaged by point (C) of Rule 65. May we also remark that SFOR and the federal police are in Vitez, so there would be no problem whatsoever, even if they were supposed to report to the police station every day, or to SFOR, or whatever you may decide. As for the danger for victims or witnesses, before the accused came to The Hague, they had spent a considerable amount of time at home after the war, and until they came to The Hague, they absolutely did not jeopardise anyone, and throughout the proceedings, not a single piece of evidence was presented that would indicate any kind of dangerous behaviour on their part after the war, and especially there would not be any such evidence after they had found out that an indictment was issued against them. Your Honours, we are in your hands, and we kindly ask you to rule on their provisional release. I believe that that would be all. Just one more thing: If you do not take our word for all these medical conditions that I referred to, we are prepared, during the course of this day or by Monday at the latest, to provide all the relevant medical documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I should like to express my satisfaction that Mr. Radovic has stated that the Prosecutor, when she met the Minister of Justice of Croatia in Zagreb, had referred her interlocutors to the Rules of Procedure, Article 65, the notion of exceptional circumstances, as well as the authority of the Trial Chamber to deal with any such requests. Mr. President, I'm told to speak more slowly. I was just saying that the Prosecutor referred her interlocutors to the Rules of Procedure, to Article 65 of those Rules, the notion of exceptional circumstances, and the authority of the Trial Chamber. And I wish to underline that yesterday, the words of Mr. Radovic were less clear as compared to what he said today. If I may be allowed, I will now go on to say that it is necessary to note that in accordance with Article 65, paragraph (B) of the Rules of Procedure, there must be absolute certainty that the released accused will appear. I wish to underline that in view of the seriousness of the charges levelled against them, and in view of the seriousness of the penalties that may be ruled if they are found guilty, I think that the Trial Chamber cannot be certain that they will appear in court if they are released. I would add that I don't think that any measure, any police measure, can guarantee their appearance if they are released and allowed to go back to their homes. Secondly, it seems to me that in accordance with Rule 65, paragraph (B), the Trial Chamber must note before making a decision on provisional release that no victim or witness or other person will be endangered by that release. I think that we are in the course of the proceedings, that all the evidence has still not been presented to the Chamber, we still have the rejoinder and rebuttal stages, and that we have submitted a motion listing the names of witnesses that we intend to call in the rebuttal stage. Therefore there is nothing to exclude any contact between the accused, if they are released and go back home, that they will not enter into contact with those witnesses. One of the witnesses appearing on this list of the Prosecution has already stated, in a written statement that the Trial Chamber is aware of, that he has been exposed to certain pressure and certain requests which he had to refuse. Therefore, it does not seem to me, in these circumstances and in view of the stage of the proceedings that we have reached, that the Trial Chamber can be convinced that other people will not be endangered by the release of the accused. Finally, the concept of exceptional circumstances prescribed by the Rules of Procedure should be understood as circumstances which are normally not expected which warrant the release of the accused. In the words of Mr. Radovic, I did not hear anything but a presentation of family difficulties, financial difficulties, and health difficulties of the members of the families of the accused. I am not doubting the reality of those problems, but it seems to me that whenever a head of a family is incarcerated, this necessarily provokes difficulties of this nature, family problems, financial problems, health problems, for the youngest members of the family in most cases. This is regrettable, and there must be ways of remedying it, but I think that we cannot, under any circumstances, consider this to be exceptional circumstances in the sense envisaged by Rule 65, paragraph (B), of the Rules of Procedure. I will gladly admit that today, these children must necessarily miss the authority of their fathers, and the lives of those families have been seriously upset, and I hope that all the assistance of their surroundings, their family, will be provided. But I do not see there a motive that can lead the Trial Chamber to accept the request of the Defence. I, therefore, request the Trial Chamber to reject the two requests for provisional release that have been made to it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just comment on what has been said by the Prosecutor regarding some general reasons why he believes that the request of the Defence should not be accepted? As for the statement that there is a possibility of influencing witnesses on the list today submitted to the Court, only one witness is mentioned who could testify to circumstances linked to the first and second of the accused. With respect to that witness, since the Prosecutor has called this witness as his witness, the Defence pledges not to have any contact with that witness. Furthermore, the Prosecutor said that there are no guarantees that the accused will reappear. I think the fact that they surrendered voluntarily disproves this because they believe that this is the place where they should prove their innocence. As for the possibility of any threats or pressure on witnesses in the course of these proceedings, in the testimony of many witnesses, even those who made the severest charges and accusations against Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, said that these were quiet people who were held in high esteem until these events, and not one of the witnesses felt that they were under any threat on their part. Even [redacted] [redacted], the witness who, indeed, had the most serious accusations against them, said that until the 16th, they were good people. So I think that we know from the record that they cannot be expected to treat witnesses in any other way but a positive one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, of course, this is a very serious matter, and we can't decide right away, more so because we have to get in touch with the relevant authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We've already had contacts with the Dutch authorities and we know their position now. But, as I say, we have to get some assurances from the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In light of all that, we will decide, I think, next week, early next week, and issue a written decision, and we will let you know. I suggest that we now resume with the witness, Vlatko Kupreskic, and we move on to cross-examination by Mr. Terrier, if he is agreeable, or Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kupreskic. You are aware of my role in these proceedings, I'm sure, and I do have some questions for you as a result of what you've been saying to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will, however, just preface that by saying that none of the references I propose to make --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would preface that by saying that none of the references I have to matters of evidence or documents, I think, go outside the parameters already set by the Chamber for such references. They will either be matters which are on the record as part of testimony in the course of trial or, in the main, in fact, they are exhibited documents already which --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: -- are already in the possession of the Chamber. So I sincerely hope there will be no difficulties as a result of any matters I put to Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, you lived in Ahmici for the whole of your life, up to the war in 1993; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: To your knowledge, are there any other people in the vicinity or in the municipality of Vitez, if you can even say that, who have the same name as yourself, "Vlatko Kupreskic"?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, of any other person bearing the same first and last name. I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you say that over the years, the Kupreskic family has become and had become a prominent family in the Ahmici/Pirici area?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know under which criteria. I don't see that it is a prominent family. It's just like any other people, both Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you say that perhaps with your cousin Ivica being in business, with yourself as an executive with the SPS company, and with your cousins, Zoran and Mirjan, involved in their cultural activities, would you say that the Kupreskic family was held in high esteem locally?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think the family was, indeed, held in high esteem. It was like a European family, and we had our neighbours, Muslims, who were also held in very high esteem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon me. You have already testified that with regard to your neighbours and, presumably, later your customers in business, you enjoyed good and civilised relations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So, sir, when, as an educated man like yourself, you saw the emergence of nationalist parties and the fact that the population then appeared to vote along very ethnic lines, did you find that a disturbing prospect?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In a sense, yes, it did disturb me because I never wanted to join a national party.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you saw the development of the political situation around you, you indicated to us that you decided to leave the SPS company partly because of the economic difficulties but partly, and I will quote you, "I saw problems with certain regulations and did not want to be in a position to violate laws." I wonder if you could explain, Mr. Kupreskic, what you meant by that expression?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I said that those laws came later on, and I was right in saying that problems would arise. As far as I remember, I didn't say that those regulations were in force, but what, indeed, did happen happened in 1992. But there could have been a contradiction in the sense that the laws of Yugoslavia were no longer respected but only the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I didn't want to be punished by such laws, since, in those days, in 1991, the International Community still recognised Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So what, just very briefly, sort of generically, what kind of laws are you referring to? Laws for the conduct of business or social laws relating to ethnic groups? What are we talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I have nothing to do with laws about ethnic or social groups. I'm referring exclusively to laws relevant to the army and business. I'm talking about economic laws, and the economic laws of Yugoslavia and those of Bosnia-Herzegovina were already on a collision course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So it seems, I believe, you said in 1991, later on around September, you, in fact, took up an offer to work with your cousin Ivica and work in the private sector; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was November in the enterprise Stefani-Bosna, as it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you have also said that Mr. Ivica Kupreskic valued your particular high level of education and experience in commercial dealing and in the handling of documentation. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. That was one of the main reasons why he invited me to join that company, because in that company, there was no other person who held such a post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, if nothing more, as a matter of curiosity, you then in due course arranged a change of name of the company. May I ask what prompted the change of name?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Another reason why Ivica asked me to join Stefani-Bosna was that that company was already going downhill, and it was blocked. When I joined, my first task was to deblock the company, which I managed to achieve. You know how things work in the west in the business world. I didn't want to work in an enterprise known for being a failure, for being blocked, and I personally proposed a change of name to Sutre and reregistered it under that new name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe, in fact, the name "Sutre," if I translate correctly, means "tomorrow"; is it right? In the English language it would.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Something like that. I don't know myself what it means. But it's not Sutre; "Sutre" is "tomorrow." Our family had the nickname Sutre, and that is why I chose it as a name. You know that it's always better to have a single word, it's easier to remember, for the name of a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you obviously had, therefore, a more positive image of the company to put forward. Is it true that, I think you have said here and you said when you spoke to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, that your main focus throughout that period of 1992 was not an interest in politics or things of that nature, but you were interested principally in business; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and it was always like that up to the war and almost so during the war and especially after the war, only business.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to just be able to confirm an impression I have and would like to offer you, that it would appear that these nationalist parties, whoever's nationalism, were parties that intolerant of people who did not support them or agree with them or who were not part of their ethnic group. Would you say that that is a correct assessment of the attitude of these political parties?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what they had in their mind and whether their thoughts were along the lines that you have just described. I just don't know because I never attended a single meeting of any such party, regardless of whether it represented the Croatian, the Muslim, or the Serb people. So I cannot judge what their positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let's say, Mr. Kupreskic, in the course of 1992, you, as a businessman and in private enterprise, had to have dealings with the municipal authorities; is that right? You needed permits and so forth.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In fact, I had rather bad relations, maybe precisely because I hadn't joined in political life and the developments in the environment. But those tasks were performed exclusively by my cousin, Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you personally did not have dealings with those authorities, but your company did; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, my company had contacts with the executive authorities in view of its tax obligations, which it has like any other firm in the business world, but when we had to settle our fiscal obligations and to make arrangements along those lines, only then did I go to the municipality, and I dealt exclusively with my colleagues, economists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But in order to function clearly through the efforts of your cousin, Ivica, the reality was that you had to have permits in order to travel, and you were, indeed, issued a general permit as a company selected to supply foodstuffs within the municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. As in 1992, there was, of course, a political executive body. Not a single able-bodied person or somebody unfit for military service, like myself, could not move around without a permit from the HVO and also without permission from the Muslim authorities, which also in 1992, I remember very well, were accommodated in the house of Enes Sehic, my teacher, so that Ivica and I would go and get both these permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In point of fact, it was important to you, was it not, that your company projected, if you like, a positive image for any of those authorities, be it the HVO or be it Muslim?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as our image and reputation is concerned, you know that in the business world, the most important thing is to have a good product and to be competitive, and that was my task in the company. I always strove towards competitiveness and nothing else. Do you think we would have got that permission if we didn't offer the best prices and if we were not in the position to be able to carry out our delivery obligations? We would never have got it otherwise. So it was exclusively guided by economic interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You don't think perhaps that the attitudes of people like the HVO would play any part in their selection of people with whom they would allow business to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think not because our firm, at a public competition, offered the best terms, and we were selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other companies that were selected to do similar work as yourselves?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know what the business of other companies was. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But it would be true to say that operating as you were in what became effectively an HVO-controlled area, your company was able to continue trading and, indeed, survive the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Our company worked in an area under the control of both the Croatian and Muslim authorities. Our market, if you like, was more focused on territory under the control of the Muslim authorities. So there's no question about it, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So from what you're saying, Mr. Kupreskic, I gain the impression that you went to considerable lengths to appear purely a non-political person and to deal equally and fairly with all, irrespective of their ethnic background. I think you said that to be so.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is certainly so. That is how I behaved, both until the 16th of April, that is how I behaved during the war, and that is how I behaved after the war, and you can verify that to this day. If you look at the composition of customers coming to the middle of Ahmici in 1994 and 1995, according to statistical figures that we have in my company, 90 per cent of those customers were Muslims, many of whom were my immediate neighbours. So you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kupreskic, you say that at the time, I think, towards the end of 1992, around December, you undertook some work on behalf of the local police; is that right? Preparing an inventory?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I started to prepare an inventory with an inventory commission. Yes, it is true. I think that was in the second half of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And this police service for whom you were working, was that in fact the police of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and did you perform that duty at -- or that work, I should say -- at the police station in Vitez? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the civilian police, the civilian police in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I believe you've referred to the boss at that place, as far as you were concerned, to be a Mr. Mirko Samir; is that right? Or is it Samija? I'm sorry; I may be wrong. Samija?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Mirko Samija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, I have jumped ahead, of course, beyond the first conflict mentioned of October 1992, but I believe you say that you had no real knowledge or part in any of that event; is that right? 20th of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not take part, absolutely, in the first conflict. It is not true that I have no knowledge; I do have knowledge. There was a conflict at the barricade down there, as I said. On that day, there were even casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But that is knowledge that you acquired later; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I've reached a kind of subject break, briefly, Your Honours. We are that close to half past 10.00, I wonder if you would like to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. So a 30-minute break? 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If I may, I should like to cut into the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Blaxill after what you just said, Mr. President, regarding the decision which is to be taken regarding the motion for provisional release. The Tribunal indicated that they expected Bosnian authorities to give some assurances. I should like to express to you the concern of the Prosecutor's office regarding the possibility -- only the possibility -- that the Bosnian Herzegovinian authorities can issue whatever assurances, or assurances in legal matters, and particularly in this particular field of legal assurances, that is, the safety of persons. Our experience with the co-operation with the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we believe that the federal authorities there simply cannot offer any guarantees in any field whatsoever with regard to police matters or judicial matters. Since the accused here are Croats from Bosnia, we do not believe that Bosnian authorities can really offer whatever guarantees, and this is, I'm afraid, still the very sad and deplorable reality in that territory, even five years after the conclusion of the accords. As for the Croat authorities, I mean Bosnian Croat authorities, we have had -- and I must tell the Court that we've run into major difficulties in trying to obtain their co-operation, and the reality and the sincerity of their commitment is really highly uncertain. I should like to inform the Tribunal, by way of information, of a letter which the Prosecutor sent to the Minister of Foreign Affairs for Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding the co-operation, the commitment of people, of liaison officers there, with the Tribunal. The representative, the liaison officer in Bosnia-Herzegovina, calumnified the Tribunal, they're trying to set one community against another community, and they never did any of the things that we asked them to do, never complied with any of our requests. I believe that in this particular case those Croat authorities, even if they do assume a commitment, we have to wait for them to -- we still have to wait for them to really comply with their commitments to do whatever they're asked. We still have to see that they sincerely will comply with this. That is, Mr. President, very briefly what I wanted to say, in order not to cut into the cross-examination for too long, but this is the view of the Prosecutor in this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, do you wish to respond to this problem regarding the assurances provided by the Bosnian Herzegovinian authorities? Of course this is a very important matter, because this is a sine qua non condition for the possible provisional release of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have nothing else to add apart from what we already said, that is, that the accused themselves will undertake to appear here whenever requested by the Tribunal. As they were the ones who volunteered to come to The Hague, they already demonstrated that they wanted to see this trial conducted and completed. You can also hear from their testimonies, if I may say so, that indeed, during all this period of time -- that is, of a year, and over a year, since they have been indicted -- and whenever they tried to establish contact with the Tribunal, they always felt very bad; they always tried to find themselves a way to turn themselves over. And from the two of them, from their own testimonies and the testimonies of witnesses, we can see that they spent all this time in the territory of Vitez. That is, they never hid. As for these relations and guarantees, naturally, if one defines things in this manner, then it completely excludes any possibility of even discussing provisional release from detention. But I nevertheless think that if one contacts the relevant persons in the Federation, and possibly the Croatian embassy in The Hague and the Bosnian embassy in The Hague, that in that case perhaps we could get some information from them, perhaps some additional information, and possibly some assurances and guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There's a little problem because we keep talking of the Croatian authorities, the Croatian Embassy. You mentioned or Counsel Radovic mentioned a meeting of our Chief Prosecutor with the Minister of Justice in Zagreb, but that is a different state. In a way, this may underline the link between Croatia and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is a problem which may have some legal relevance for other matters. I wondered to what extent the Croatian authorities in Zagreb are in a position to give guarantees or assurances? Anyway, we will take into consideration this letter from the Prosecutor to the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you, Mr. Terrier, and we may now proceed. Since we are still now discussing matters other than the cross-examination, I wonder whether Mr. Blaxill minds my asking a question to him and Mr. Terrier about the document we received actually this morning, the Prosecutor's submission of rebuttal witnesses. There is one point which I would like to clarify as soon as possible. In point 4 of this letter, signed by Mr. Terrier and Mr. Blaxill, it is stated that the Prosecution anticipates that the time required to finalise the written closing arguments be four weeks from the close of all evidence. Now, this has an impact on our programme for the future and also on other trials. Do you mean to say that if we start again on the 27th, probably we will need two weeks, one week for the Prosecution and probably one week for the Defence, and the Defence will have some rejoinder witnesses, and after that, you need four weeks to prepare for the closing statements? So that means that there will again be a gap. So we will then have a four-week recess before the closing arguments? Because we were thinking of having the closing arguments immediately after the closure of the Defence case. I, for one, was wrong then. You want to have this gap of about four weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, indeed, after the rejoinder, that is, the last witness for the Defence, we should, indeed, like to have some time for reflection. Four weeks, perhaps you think that is too -- if you think that that is too long, of course, we could cut it shorter, but we shall need some recess between the rejoinder and the final arguments. I do really think that it is important because the Prosecutor, of course, also needs to reflect about the case, and we need to do that in this difficult case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But you will be submitting the text in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We shall present first a summary, a concise and clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Also short?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: With references?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, with references to all the exhibits. We shall do that, and we shall submit the extended version in writing, of course, and there will be, of course, an oral presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, you have two months to do that. There will only be a handful of witnesses. Surely you don't need a month, an additional month. You have until the 27th of September to prepare all of that. A day or two should be sufficient to make the additions, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I concede that perhaps this is quite a comfortable period of time that we're requesting, yes, I admit that, but I think that we, nevertheless, need a certain period of time to complete our written text which, of course, is already being prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So the Defence will be entitled to the same recess, so that we shall have to adjourn for two to three weeks. Four perhaps is too much. But then two or three weeks, yes, so that the Defence can also prepare its closing argument so that we shall have only the final part, that is, the closing argument at the end, both of the Prosecution and the Defence; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if possible, we should like the Prosecution, particularly if they complete their closing argument earlier, to submit it to us a week before we do that, that is, the summary, I mean, because in our closing argument, we should also like to touch upon some topics and some problems which will perhaps figure in the text of the Prosecution. So could we have this text at least one week before the final deadline?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think this would be fair, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I do apologise to Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic and to Mr. Blaxill, but if you don't mind, we would like to finish with this matter. Let me suggest a sort of tentative schedule. We will resume on the 27th of September, and the Prosecution will need four working days, I understand, from their document for the -- what did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: From what we heard, we got the interpretation that we would be finished by the 27th of September, and we knew it was just the beginning, the 27th is the beginning rather than the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will resume on the 27th of September, and then four working days for the Prosecution, and then we will go on until the 7th of October, and there will be five working days for the Defence for any rejoinder witnesses. So we will stop on the 7th. Then we will give three weeks to the Prosecution for their closing statements, their final brief, and four weeks to the Defence. So the Prosecution should submit their written brief by the 29th of October, whereas the Defence should submit their brief by the 5th of November. This is what Counsel Slokovic-Glumac suggested. You will have one more week, and in that week, you can meet some of the points made by the Prosecution in their written brief. Then we would resume our hearings on the 8th of November for closing statements, and probably we will need, say, not more than three days, I assume, for closing arguments, so the 8th, 9th, and 10th of November. As I say, it's a tentative plan. Would that suit you, Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Only a comment. We're told that the accused, Dragan Papic, will also be testifying, and I suppose that will be after the rebuttal witnesses; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. Yes, indeed. First, Dragan Papic, and then your witnesses, four witnesses, and then the witnesses called by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, would you agree? Yes. Let us stick to this tentative plan. However, we have to stick to this plan because, as you know, Judge May is sitting in another trial, and he has to revise the whole schedule. So, therefore, we can't now change it again. All right. Again, my apologies to Mr. Blaxill and to Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. Mr. Blaxill, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, with your leave, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, if we can get back to what we were talking about, sir, just before the break and the subsequent argument, you were working for a period in the police station in Vitez in late 1992, early 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but may I explain how it came about for my part-time work for the police? Sometime in December, I was at a wedding, and there I met, quite by chance, with the then head of the police station, Mr. Mirko Samija. He approached me and we talked, and he told me, he asked me to come and try, as it was the end of the business year, that I should come and help them take the stock, the inventory, at the police station and to make a statement of accounts and a kind of a balance sheet, as there was nobody in the police station who would know how to do it professionally, according to standard. He was a very capable man, a competent man. He graduated from law; I even believe he was a judge. He'd also joined that police station only a short time before that, and he wanted to put things in order there. I told him that it was practically impossible because I was working for the Sutre company, and then we agreed that I would come part time, for an hour or two, for a day or whatever, when I could. That was the only way in which I agreed to such an agreement, and that is what I did in the latter half of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Whilst you were doing this work, this inventory work at Vitez police station, did you, in fact, come across anybody else with a name similar to yours or, indeed, identical to your own?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that. In the municipality of Vitez, I did not meet anyone with any namesake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you undertake or were you requested to undertake any other duties or assistance to the police whilst you were there between December 1992 and February 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, absolutely not because, to begin with, I had not been trained for that kind of work. Secondly, I did not have enough time because I worked for another company. Thirdly, I never undertook to do any other work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would like to show you just a couple of documents, Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: These have been duly served on the Defence, Your Honours. We have all the appropriate copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 377 of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could I just clarify if under that number of 377, that includes both documents, one dated the 28th of December, 1992 and the other dated the 23rd of February, 1993, or is it just the one, just to be sure?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. I thought there was only one document. So the first document will be 377 of the 28th of December, 1992, and the other one dated the 23rd of February, 1993 will be 378.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We didn't get the February document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, do you have those documents in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Right. They should be on their way. Do you have in front of you now, Mr. Kupreskic, a document issued apparently from the Travnik police administration on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and dated the 28th of December, 1992? Is that before you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have a document entitled "Report" from the 22nd of February, 1993, and it's exactly the same. I have two identical copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just hold on, Mr. Kupreskic, we will have that changed.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the 28th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And, sir, if you look at the bottom of the first page, you'll see some names, or at least in my translation there are. The first, number 1, Mirko Samija. That is the man you've referred to, is it not, in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It then purports, that document, to set out a number of names and their roles in the police force; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. This list continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you look on the last page, at entry number 55 in that list of names. Would you tell me what it says, please, number 55.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is my name and surname, and it says "Operative officer for the prevention of crimes of particular state interest -- inspector."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So that would appear, as you say it is your name, Mr. Kupreskic, that you were not, surely, just doing an inventory for the police over a short period of time. What can you say about this apparent role you had as an operative officer for the prevention of crimes of particular state interest?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this is the explanation I give, and this is the way it is. The budget of every state provides resources for social services, including the police. May I say first and foremost that I never got a document of appointment, because that is not the agreement we had. I agreed with the chief of police that I would do this job on an ad hoc basis. However, in order to be able to pay me for the job I would do, they had to include me in their job descriptions; they had to assign me to a particular post in the police station so that they could pay me from the resources that were allocated to them, and that is probably why the chief of police, Mirko Samija, included me in this post. You can see by the number, 55, that that is the very last post, and it was probably a vacant post at the time, so formally he just assigned me there -- that is to say, within the job descriptions of the police station -- so that he could pay me. But I never got any document of appointment to that particular job, to the best of my recollection. I do not even remember having received this compensation for having made out these inventories. Secondly, I never did this kind of job, nor do I know how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, were you aware at the time that this gentleman was going to put you on the roster of the police with such a title, or let us say abuse the system in this way? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. This is the first time I see this here. I did not know at all how he or, rather, the police station, would pay me for services rendered. I believe that that is the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And so even -- we move on to document 378, please, the next document, a report dated the 22nd of February, 1993. This was compiled on an inspection of Vitez police station, so it says, and was an inspection by officers of police administration based in Travnik, in other words, acting on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. You are referred to, are you not, in that document of the 22nd of February, 1993, as -- and if I quote correctly, as I'm reading from a translation -- "... and the function of officer for the prevention of crimes of particular state interest is being performed by Vlatko Kupreskic." Now, that would appear to be a fairly serious official report of an alleged function performed by you, in an official government document, sir. Have you any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, I was not there when those people came and when they toured the police station, and I was not at this meeting, so to speak. So this is simply a formal report that they must have taken from the job description sheet, and then, as they were checking on the overall situation, they found in this job description, they found my name too. Let me just say one thing. I never interrogated anyone. I never made a single note. I never did that. Formally, I was assigned to the office of the crime prevention service. I was assigned a desk where I would work with the commission for making inventories of basic supplies. For that I did not receive any document of appointment either. So I was just formally assigned to that office, and as I said, probably in order to provide me with compensation, the chief of police, Mirko Samija, probably appointed me to this vacant post in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now can we put another document I think has already been handed in, that of the 1st of March? No? It's coming. "A plan for March," it is entitled, dated the 1st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 379.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, this is just a document entitled "A plan for March," as I've said, dated the 1st of March, 1993; you would agree with that? It was signed by Mr. Anto Bajric, I believe; did you know that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, never, until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. So you look in that document, and it would appear that the duties and tasks of people working in that particular field are very much those of making -- essentially monitoring information and collating evidence and information, very much a clerical task rather than one of perhaps being an interrogator or anything like that. But were you aware of the activities of that department, at least?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No. There is no mention of me here, or of my name. Secondly, after the 25th of February 1993, I never even stopped by the police station. I never dropped into the building of the police station until the end of the war. Allow me to say that I managed somehow, with great difficulty, to complete the inventory, and then I decided, I think in two days, to give this inventory, this report, and I left the police station. However, on the 27th of February, 1993, some -- I don't know what he did; some person called Zute, his name was Zarko Andric, attacked that police station, and he beat up almost all the people who worked in that police station. After that, I telephoned. I didn't even want to go to see Mr. Mirko Samija, and I said that I did not want to go to that police station any more. Simply, I completed the inventory, although I did not know whether I had the final balance of accounts, but I said that I did not want to come to the police station again, and indeed, I did not do that all the way until the end of the war. I have witnesses to that effect too. I have this witness, this Muslim who did the inventory with me, and that is Mr. Muhamed Trako. I also have Mr. Miro Azarovic as my witness, a Serb, who at that time was chief of the crime prevention service, which is a post I think he holds until the present day. At the time when I was making the inventory and compiling this balance of accounts, across the room from me was a man called Sejo, I think, a Muslim who held a university degree too, and he was a friend of mine as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kupreskic. Let's move on, shall we, to the days preceding what has been described as the second conflict and we know was the worst event to occur in Ahmici. Now, you are saying, sir, that prior to the 16th of April, 1993, you undertook a business trip to Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 14th of April, 1993, I went -- we went primarily to pick up Ankica Kupreskic, Ivica Kupreskic's wife. At the same time, we went on a business trip in order to cover our expenses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In fact, you have already produced to this Court, have you not, the document that gave you free travel from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO, which you obtained on the 13th of April? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. The document for travel issued by the company was dated the 13th of April, and the document of the HVO on the movement of persons was issued on the 14th of April 1993, and it is only on the basis of that travel document -- that is to say, the HVO document -- that one could travel, one could get out of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In point of fact, was that the document that was stamped at the border crossing at Metkovic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perhaps D26/3 could be shown to the witness, if you would be so kind, and maybe at the same time D24/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, there's one document, and it in fact bears a date stamp, border crossing, 14/04/93, Metkovic. Do you have that there, Mr. Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was that in fact your HVO permission to have the free travel throughout Herceg-Bosna and perform the business trip, Vitez to Split and back to Vitez? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not right. I shall briefly repeat, we got general approval from the municipality for supplying the municipality with basic food and supplies. On the basis of this general approval and permission that my Defence showed here, we were entitled to receive this permit for the movement of persons, and its number is 1288-04/93. Then the documents are issued as follows. First of all, a travel order for a business trip from the company when we wish to travel, and we did that, that is to say, on the 13th of April, 1993. It says here that the trip was supposed to last for four days. So then, on the basis of this travel order form from the enterprise, we got an order from the HVO or, rather, this permit for the movement of persons. This permit issued by the HVO is what we have to show when we exit Vitez. That was in Novi Travnik, that is to say, it's at a checkpoint, a roadblock. We show it to the military there, they take a look at it, and they let us go on that business trip. This same document was requested at the Metkovic border crossing. So Ivica and I both, both of us had, had these permits issued by the HVO. On his document and on mine there is a stamp of the border crossing of Metkovic in the upper right-hand corner, and indeed, we did cross the border at the Metkovic border crossing, as it says here on the stamp, that is to say, on the 14th of April, 1993. I have the same permit that Ivica Kupreskic got. There was no other way you could move through Central Bosnia towards the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
