utterances.text: The other document you have there, sir, of course, I think, is a different type of document, because that is the one you've referred to as a document raised within your own company creating the business trip and thus justifying your expenses in the company's books; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Precisely. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, you encountered somebody on that journey who was known to you. We're talking of a protected witness, so I will not use the name, and I would ask you not to, but there was a person who was driving and encountered you, you say, at a fuel station, and you say in evidence it was on the 14th of April on your way to Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 14th of April, 1993, we encountered, at the gasoline station, the witness who had testified here under the pseudonym DE on the 6th of May, 1999. This person was not driving. We found this person at the gasoline station. This person's truck was parked on the opposite side, as far as I can remember now, in the town of Pocitelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, do you recall keeping, in 1993, what you entitled as a war diary and was a document, in fact, that was seized from the briefcase that was taken from you when you were arrested? Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I kept a war diary, and, indeed, it was most welcome for me so that I have it today to show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We can check this later, as we will be putting this document formally into the Court, to the Chamber, and we'll all be seeing it, but there's just an entry, I see, that you made admittedly in August of 1996, that you made an entry in that diary regarding certain people and places and referred to that person we know as DE with the quote "saw us in Pocitelj near Capljina on 15 April, 1992, on the eve of the war." Now, that would appear to be a different recollection when you entered your diary to the date that you gave this Tribunal yesterday in your oral evidence. Can you explain that discrepancy to us, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We -- I certainly saw the mentioned person in Pocitelj on the 14th of April, 1993, and how I entered this in my diary, that, I cannot say now. I cannot remember unless you show me the diary. I wrote this in 1996 or 1997 when I was, in fact, preparing my defence, because I know 100 per cent that we saw this friend, this Muslim, at that particular place. So perhaps this is an omission, but you did not show this to me. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, obviously to assist you in clarifying this, we will now put this document in to the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There will be some references to this war diary in the course of my cross-examination, Your Honours. I would therefore recommend we keep it close to hand. Secondly, there will be on occasion, I think, some little difficulty or time lag in reaching the references because we have a paginated translation and this was a handwritten document by Mr. Kupreskic; therefore, clearly the page numbers would not be in sync at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, would you turn, please, to the entries you made on the 7th of August -- I'm just looking beyond -- it's between the 31st of July, 1996 entry and the next entry which you made on the 8th of August, 1996. Can you see item number 14 in that passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honours, it's page 16 for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Are you referring to the part where I wrote that I saw this person in Pocitelj on the 15th of April, 1992? I found that page, and it says that I saw that person on the 15th of April, 1992. I even wrote here "on the day of the war," and there was no war then. Because I thought this was quite unimportant then, when I was preparing my defence. Well, listen, try to understand this: Who can remember exactly three or four years back?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The translation that was made into the English language says "the eve of the war," and the expression "eve," to us, means the day before. So that, in fact, would be a correct entry. The 15th of April was the eve of the war. So is there a translation problem? Because you've just said "the day of the war."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can only say to you that this is an informal document, first and foremost. When I was preparing for my defence, of course, I was writing out a basic draft. Only later when I got into these documents and when I saw the orders, then I saw that I encountered this person on the 14th of April, which only corroborates what this diary says, that I'm saying the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kupreskic, we shall move on from there. You went into Split, you did business, and you say you returned to Ahmici on the 15th of April, 1993; that is correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I returned to Ahmici on the 15th of April, 1993, around 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are you precisely sure? You said "around," so you're not precise to the minute, but are you sure regarding the time? Was it 7.00 p.m.? Was it perhaps a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's hard to tell now, six or seven years later, with accuracy, but I know that it was early evening, I know that the shop was closed, so I think that it was about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall an occasion, I think it was the 11th of June, 1998, when you had an interview with my learned colleagues, Mr. Terrier and Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I say to you, sir, and we will show this to you later, that you indicated to them that you arrived home at around 8.00 p.m. that evening, because, as you stated, "It was already getting dark. I'm sure it was around that time," how do you now perhaps account for this apparent at least one-hour discrepancy in your memory?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, when we were having that conversation, at that time, I thought that such things were quite insignificant, and you will find in this transcript that that is what I said to the Prosecutor, Mr. Terrier. Are those things important? Isn't it much more important that I was never a soldier, that I never had a weapon? Isn't it important that I was two kilometres away from the site of the events. I considered those things to be important. But now when I have been drawn into this trial, of course, I realise now that these things are important for you, and I have tried to refresh my memory. So I think it was a little earlier, but around 7.00 p.m. It's so difficult to tell. You must understand. So much time has passed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So we shall have to leave that as a discrepancy, sir. You have been saying to us that you considered certain things insignificant, so does that question of significance judge the accuracy of your memories? In other words, if you judged something not to be significant in your eyes, do you give a casual or uncalculated reply to that, or do you take care to try and be accurate?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I tried to tell the truth and I have told the truth. But as regards time, whether I was quite accurate, who can be? You see, your Witness L said first that he saw me on that day at 3.00, then at 4.00, then later on, he said at 6.00, towards evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, you have told us that on the 15th, when you got back, you went straight home, you parcelled up some goods ready to deliver to, I think it was, Travnik, if I'm correct, the following day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't stop on the way. We came straight to my house, unloaded the goods. Later on, my wife and I carried those goods upstairs. We had to stick the labels onto the jeans, Levi's 501s, for this customer in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: After that, you went to bed. Did you have any other sort of social contact with anybody that evening or did you just stay home with your wife?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My wife and I finished the work we had. Of course, we wrote out an invoice for this customer as well, and I wanted to go to bed as soon as possible. But sometime about 8.00 in the evening, I informed this buyer in Travnik that the next day, the 16th of April, 1993, in the morning, I would bring the goods before 8.00, the goods that he had ordered a couple of days previously. Then we all went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: By that reply, sir, do you mean that you did not have any social contact with anybody else after you had arrived home that evening, the 15th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, absolutely no one came to visit us in the house, in front of the house, nor did we go anywhere. I was terribly tired. I wanted to get what we had left to do done so that I could leave early in the morning and deliver the goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You said that early in the morning of the 16th of April, you were awoken by your wife, and we've heard there was an unknown voice telling you to get out and go to a shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, did your wife -- I'm sorry. After speaking to that person, did you hear them say anything else as to a reason for going to a shelter?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely not, but the receiver was hung up immediately. But this had happened previously too, so I considered it to be a provocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Subsequently, Mr. Ivica Kupreskic telephoned you, you clearly believed there was a problem, and you duly made your way from your home towards the shelter. That would be the sequence of events, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. After that, Ivica called up, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you informed us that your wife had spoken to you at that time, when the first or second call -- I think the first call came in, and she said that somebody had called at about 3.00 in the morning but she hadn't wanted to disturb you. Did your wife tell you what that caller had said?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The same, what this other person said at 5.00. But let me describe a situation in connection with these calls, telephone calls. I heard that some Muslims would inform Croats and they would go to a shelter for no reason and vice versa. Even these things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, to go back to the war diary that's still with you, and in the same place, the same section where you have the writing about that encounter on the journey at item 14, would you read item 20, please?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The diary will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 380.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I can just remind you, Mr. Kupreskic, it's the section of writing, I think, under the 31st of July, 1996. The entry that follows it is the 8th of August, 1996, if that helps to get you back to the page.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 31st of July, 1996, is it on that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is, indeed. If you look down to item 20 --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: -- there's a reference to a person called Vlatko Matosevic, if I read that correctly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me just find it. I beg your pardon. I can't find it. I can't find the page. Could you help me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think we have one that's marked.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As there are no ordinal numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honours. Again I refer to page 16.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Item number 20, Vlatko Matosevic, what is the entry that you've written there, and can you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Witness," "Pirici." It says "Witness" and then it says "Pirici." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Item 20, as it reads in our translation, the line below it reads: "Stated that it was possible that he had telephoned at 0500 hours about withdrawal." Are those words there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then we haven't got a correct entry, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, under number 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Number 20. Thank you. And those words are there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are they followed by the words "and put his rifle to my neck in Pirici"? What, pray, would that mean?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, when I reached the Zume outpatient's clinic, I was sent to Pirici to take some medicines and bandages, and this was the first day when I reported. So driving my own car, I took that material, but for about 50 metres, it was not possible to go by car, so I went on foot. At that moment, this person met me whom I did not know, nor did he know me at the time, and as I was on my way back towards the car, he probably thought that I was fleeing from the front line, and that is why I mentioned him here, that he could testify how I had come to that health centre and what he did to me. So he could say what I did and that I wasn't at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, we've heard several witnesses who have appeared in the course of this trial. They made mention of seeing some HVO kind of people in uniforms and so forth in the vicinity of the Kupreskic houses during the day of the 15th. But it is true to say, is it not, Mr. Kupreskic, that clearly you were not there so have no personal experience as to whether any HVO were in Ahmici or not during the 15th; is that right? Because you were in Split.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, I was in another state, whereas in my house and near my house, there were no military men. Neither did they come, neither did they appear, neither did my wife tell me anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, the fact is if you were in another state, you were out on the road travelling and were not in Ahmici between the 14th and 7.00 on the 15th, what I'm saying is you have no personal knowledge to say whether or not some HVO people visited that area. You can't say. You weren't there.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, I didn't know, nor could I see, nor did I hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I don't know if you were planning a 12.15-type of break. I've hit a subject matter that would be convenient for that purpose if you wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No. Since we have to stop at 1.00, I would go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I can also encourage you to the idea I shall not be a dramatically long period now, so I think our timing for today would be more than ample, if that's any encouragement, Your Honours. I'll try and be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, you say you made your way down to the shelter of Jozo Vrebac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you left your father at the family home because he refused to go, he didn't want to go?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He stayed behind in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did your father say why he was content to stay in the house? Did he say anything about, "Well, we have nothing to fear. We know everybody. There's no danger to us," did he say anything like that to you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, when I came to fetch them, he wasn't ready, and he said to me, "I'm not going. I'm an old man." Whether he said something else to the effect, "No one will hurt us," it's possible, but I can't remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You, as I say, leave with your family. What were you wearing at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had civilian clothing. I had a jacket, a winter jacket, trousers, shoes or boots, I don't remember exactly, a shirt. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall the colour and/or fabric of the jacket?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can because that jacket was something I wore around the house, and I think it was a chocolate colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And do you recall the material and colour of your trousers that you wore that day?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that my trousers were corduroy, greyish green, perhaps; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You arrived at the shelter, and you have said that, I believe, if I've noted your evidence correctly, you stayed there until at least 9.00; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I stayed in the shelter until 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: 10.00. And at that time, there had been continual firing? Since your arrival at the shelter, you had heard firing the whole time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the whole time. Outside and inside one could hear the shooting, and it was very heavy shooting, very loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you in fact leave the building at all prior to 10.00? Did you, in other words, go out of the shelter for any period of time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I went out for the first time about 9.30, because it was calming down a little bit, the shooting. I think a couple of other men went out, because we were always curious to see what was happening. We didn't know what it was, and I think the first time we went out was about 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So presumably you were extremely concerned as regards the fate and the condition of your father, who had been left behind at home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course I was concerned, because that was the first time in my life to experience such shooting, and I said in the shelter, "My God, this is real war."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, whilst you -- well, when you arrived at the shelter, or in fact when you left the shelter, did you see in Zume, there, the presence of any Croat soldiers or military units, defensive bunkers, or anything of that nature, set up to protect the Zume area from attack? Did you see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say you personally had not seen any of the soldiers who had gone up into Ahmici that morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I hadn't seen any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Had you been told by anybody that they had seen soldiers and who those soldiers were, where they came from?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I heard that for the first time from Niko Sakic, in his house, in his kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you went down to the shelter, had you been given any indication that the area was coming under attack, possibly by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know anything. I wanted to get the first information from my cousin, Ivica. However, I didn't find him in front of the houses, so I became even more scared, and we hastened towards the shelter even faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did the possibility of, quote, "a Mujahedin attack" cross your mind at all?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall with precision, but I think, in flight -- I can't claim whether this thought occurred to me, because I had heard, earlier on, reports on Mujahedin attacks from Barin Gaj, from the forest, and we were always afraid of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Because wasn't at least the local rumour, wasn't that the concept that the Mujahedin were fearsome individuals who would kill people, and you just didn't want the Mujahedin coming to your village; isn't that right? Is that what the rumour was?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were such bad rumours about Mujahedins. They were people from outside, that they are prone to brutal acts, and we were all afraid of them. I think even our neighbours, Muslims, were scared of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm just finding a little difficulty understanding at this point, Mr. Kupreskic, that whatever your father may have said about remaining behind, you actually left him there when there is something perhaps going to happen that could be extremely dangerous to people. Now, did you not try and persuade him to go with you, or say you would help him, or carry him, or do whatever, to get him out of that area?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that moment, it never occurred to me, because I had hoped that he would be ready. When I came down for the first time, he didn't say to me whether he was going or not. However, I was most surprised by the call of Ivica Kupreskic. Everyone had gone. So, simply, I never thought about it. I just picked up my children and went off towards Ivica Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say that later in the day you did endeavour to return to the property and did indeed get back and see your father?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, at great risk and with great effort. I travelled for almost three hours from the shelter to my house, and around 1.00, I managed to see my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was it not true, though, that some members of your community were able to move around in that area during the course of that morning, and they had not taken several hours to do so? Wasn't Mr. Ivica Kupreskic out and about, himself, during that period?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I'm not aware of where Ivica Kupreskic was nor what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you encounter him at all during that day?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember seeing him or meeting him that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let's go right through to the evening: 6.00, 7.00, 8.00 that evening of the 16th. You still say, do you, that you did not meet Mr. Ivica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps in the evening, in the shelter, he may have come, but it is very difficult for me to recollect these things. Possibly sometime in the evening, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, with what was going on in the vicinity, surely you would remember meeting someone who is your relative and to all intents and purposes also your employer? You would surely have remembered meeting Mr. Ivica Kupreskic in the course of that day, would you not?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly I would remember, in the course of that day, at the most critical time. But I couldn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I were to say to you that it is a matter of record here -- you may recall it yourself; you heard him testify -- that he saw you once that day, at about 6.00 p.m., out of the front of the Vrebac shelter? And Mr. Ivica Kupreskic also said that he had telephoned you earlier -- which we know -- but that he had seen a group of soldiers, and that you should take your family to that shelter. He actually mentioned seeing soldiers. Now, on those two points, do you have a comment, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what Ivica saw, how, and whom. It's possible that we saw each other in the shelter around 6.00. I told you that I can't remember with certainty. I said it was quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There are two specific facts here, Mr. Kupreskic; I would like you to address your mind to these as specific facts. One, that you and he encountered each other outside the Vrebac shelter at about 6.00 p.m. Is that true or is that false?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It would be perhaps true, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Ivica Kupreskic also stated that when he had telephoned you earlier that day, he mentioned having seen a group of soldiers, and that you and your family should also go to the shelter. Now, the fact I want you to focus on: Did Ivica Kupreskic say that he had seen a group of soldiers, or did he not say that, when you spoke to him on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did not tell me that on the phone. But whether he saw some soldiers and called me, having seen them, that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We've heard put to you, indeed, by Mr. Krajina, the various sightings that were alleged against you during the course of the 16th of April, 1993, put, I might add, so fairly by Mr. Krajina. I don't propose to comment on them, because he very accurately described what those witnesses said or at least I think so. What I can't understand, Mr. Kupreskic, is this. You were on such good terms with the Muslims in that area, you've lived there all your life, your home is surrounded by Muslim houses, your relatives are around you, you are respected in business; why are you being accused by all these different people who knew you so well? It can't be because you owned a house in a strategic position, can it, Mr. Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that is not so, and I repeat, I think that I'm being accused only because my Muslim neighbours could not -- just as I could not recognise those soldiers, neither could they, and they are accusing me only because I was their next-door neighbour, because my house is there, and because evidently there was gunfire from the house or around the house. I see no other reason, nor is there any other reason. All the more so as I have never, any gesture of mine, anything that I did, would move in that direction or show that I could do something like that. But couldn't you see, Mr. Prosecutor, that six Muslims from Ahmici came here and testified in my defence, on my account? You will see that there are 30 testimonies of witnesses, Muslims defend me. I have accurate statistics: 54 Defence witnesses here testified pro those facts that I quote as showing that I'm not guilty, and the Prosecution had only 57 witnesses to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't think, with respect, Mr. Kupreskic, the numbers are that important. What I'm suggesting is this: Is it not a very curious thing, when you express that there are such good relations so close around you, that so many people would indeed be putting that allegation to you? But let us move on from there, sir. What I would like to do now, if I may, is turn to the one incident that involved --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor, but this is an insult. I am accused by only one witness, Witness U, for only a split second, that he saw me with a rifle. Not any other witness ever said that he saw me with weapons or that I had done anything wrong. And then Witness L, who describes military in my house, he is a mentally-ill person, and there is only one person who is accusing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, I'd like to move, actually, to the testimony of Witness Q. Do you recall who that was?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sure I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you heard what he and his relatives said about their endeavours to escape to Upper Ahmici, passing the vicinity of your house, and mentioning your presence there with that of some uniformed soldiers. You do recall that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not, because I was not there, and therefore I cannot recall it, because I was not there. And if you mean whether I remember that they said that, yes, I did. Perhaps I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it precisely. Now --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I mean, the previous question really upset me, and -- and they said -- yes, yes, they did. I understood what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, the people made that allegation against you, they included people who knew your family very well, direct neighbours, indeed. Is that correct, sir? Please take your time, Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they are my direct neighbours. Pezers are my next-door neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There is, in fact, then a quotation in the course of what these people were saying, that there was some shouting to them, and this one person turned around and looked, and I think -- to encapsulate their evidence, very small -- with some astonishment recognised their neighbour, Vlatko Kupreskic, there with those people. Now, sir, again, I'm going to ask you: First, you were on good terms with these people. Is that right? Prior to the war, obviously.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was, normal, good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So, again, why do they say, "I turned, and to my amazement, it's my neighbour, Vlatko, with a gun, with these guys, and the people are shooting at us"? I find that a very difficult thing to understand, Mr. Kupreskic. I would like you to try and perhaps say why this person -- not just that "The locals were going to blame us," but why him? Why him?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I already answered that question. I am also astonished that of 14 persons, only that person saw me, and also for a split second. I don't think that that person is telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay, sir, thank you. That's an answer. You did pay a visit back to your family home during the course of that morning, or around lunchtime, I think you said, and when you arrived, there were soldiers at your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I found soldiers in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you discovered those soldiers, were they easily identifiable? In other words, did you know precisely whose army they were when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not right away. When I saw the first soldier, I couldn't even guess, nor did I know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How, sir, could you judge the safety factor of making an approach, as you did, to those soldiers, if you didn't know who they were? What were your feelings for your own safety at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're quite right. The risk was really big. But for some three or four hours, I was feeling this incredible -- this very powerful instinct for my parent, and perhaps it just prevailed. Of course, when I saw the soldiers, of course I was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm finding, as a result, your description of your movements somewhat difficult, sir. You say that you are down at a shelter from around 6.00 in the morning; you are concerned for your father, who was left behind in the family home, and yet you don't go back there until 1.30, or 1.00, whenever you say the time was, around lunchtime. You don't go back to that house, and yet at that time, you seem prepared to run the risk. Now, what was the difference in danger for the hours you were sheltering and the risk you were now running, approaching unknown soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Why, I felt all the time this urge: What to do, how to do it, what should I do, how to go to fetch my father, but that was impossible. Then it lasted, and there was this clash with my wife and my children -- "Don't go, you'll get killed" -- and it was only around 10.00 when the gunfire subsided a little, and I was looking for the right moment. I thought that would be the right moment; however, I was wrong. Because when I came close, and that is about a kilometre that I had to cover, when I came closer from Niko Sakic's house, then I truly realised what kind of gunfire it was, what kind of detonations they were, and then I simply did not move forward, not at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: All right. But you eventually make your approach to the house, and you are challenged by a soldier who sees you; is that right? Or did you call to him?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw him first. He did not see me because he was watching, observing other points, perhaps more interesting. But I had nothing -- I had no choice. I was scared stiff. So I just surrendered; I raised my arms and said, "I am Vlatko Kupreskic." I said also that I was the resident of that house and that I had come to fetch my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you were the first to speak; you spoke to the soldier first. Is that right? If I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I was the first one to do that. I glimpsed him straight away, because he was doing with his head left and right, and he was bound to see me within a second or two. So I just shouted out quickly, "I'm Vlatko Kupreskic," and he just pointed his rifle at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It quickly became apparent to you that he was a Croat soldier, or Bosnian Croat soldier, and that he presumably identified you by your name and however else as being of Croatian descent, so he then took you into the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it is not right. I also glimpsed him by chance, and I simply had no other choice, because he had a weapon, and I didn't know what kind of weapon, what army it was, what soldier it was, until I entered the house and saw them. Even then, when he told me to come near, I wasn't looking at him. I dared not look at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But certainly no harm came to you, and you were escorted into the house by the soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, now I can make a guess as to why he took me into the house. He just told me, "Follow me." It's because my father was inside. He was not on the ground floor, where my father usually lives. My father was upstairs. Later on, afterwards, I asked my father why he was upstairs, how did it happen that he got up there? Because he couldn't move easily around. And he told me that whilst he was still on the ground floor, that he had noticed the military ransacking houses, taking things out, and thinking that he would protect the house against this pillage if he moved to the first floor. So he somehow managed to climb to the first floor, but they did not look at anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, when you got inside the house, your father was in fact obviously very distressed, but he was at least safe, was he not?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think -- I don't think he was safe. I think he was in danger, and so was I, because those people hardly said a word. They looked so terrible. I even saw a bayonet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Kupreskic, more simply, would be nobody had shot or harmed your father in that house when you got there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is. No, nobody did him any harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Nobody offered any violence to you or to your father whilst you remained in the house with him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is right. They did no harm to me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And perhaps the only drama that occurred was when, it seems, an UNPROFOR tank came by and the HVO soldiers dived to the floor, and they dragged you down with them, until the tank had gone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was quite dramatic, but they all went down to the floor in both rooms. I couldn't understand why he pulled me down from the chair, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you made reference to somebody using a Motorola just before that incident when they dived on the floor. I could have made an erroneous note of what I heard you say. Would you please repeat what it was you heard was said by the man using the Motorola?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember ever recounting what this man said. I just don't remember. I don't think I ever mentioned that. I don't know about that. But at that time, I was just too afraid to remember things like that. Besides, I dare not focus on listening to him because I thought it might be too dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, that's a remark then that will have to remain lost on both of us, Mr. Kupreskic. Now, sir, you described the interior of your property when you got there, and I believe you mentioned that there were goods strewn about, that some soil from pots had been tossed on the carpet, and the place looked a bit ransacked. Is that a fair description by me as to what you said?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to describe it, and it would be a waste of time, but everything was topsy-turvy, that is true. Subsequently, I learned from my father what they told him, "Why is there no money here? Where is it? Where is the money? This is a rich house. How is it that there is no money here?" They were trying to force him to bring the money out, but that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. Thank you, sir. Mr. Kupreskic, can you tell me, sir, whether the windows of that building were intact when you got to your house on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not say that, nor could I see that, but afterwards --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No. I was asking you whether the windows were intact when you got to your house on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those windows in those two rooms, I can only talk about them, they were not damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: They were not damaged. Was there the presence of any other military personnel in any other of the rooms in the house?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I have yet another floor and I have other rooms on that same floor, but I did not see, nor did I dare move about. I only saw those two rooms because we had a sliding door and it was open and it was already broken and it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If you did not go to the upper floor, did you hear any sound of boots tramping about or sounds of movement or the presence of persons on the upper floor?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not hear anything truly, but considering the fear that I was experiencing, whether I could see anything or hear anything, but I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say, sir, that the two rooms that you've referred to, that had been taken over by these soldiers, those two rooms, I presume, had doors, did they? I mean, they weren't open archways. Did they have doors?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those two rooms had three doors, two front doors, two doors from which one entered, and then one door between them, a sliding door, a sort of folding door between those two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I realise you've described stressful circumstances, but did you notice the condition of the doors in those rooms when you went into your house? Had they been damaged?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those two rooms, no, the doors to those two rooms were not damaged, no, not at that time when I was there, as far as I can recollect. But I didn't really look at the door, yet I don't think they were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will be referring later, and we will look at certain sections of your interview that I've referred to with Mr. Terrier back in June 1998, but you appeared to have said to him in an interview: "I found my father who was frightened and crying. The house was devastated and destroyed." Now, in the part you say has been occupied by soldiers, I would suggest to you, sir, that hardly warrants the description of "devastated" or "destroyed," unless this is purely a linguistic difference that we have a problem with?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, quite. You're using different terms. The damage was assessed, I think, totalling some 25.000 German marks, we submitted it here as one of the exhibits for the Defence, by the assessment agency, and this can show you what kind of damage the house suffered. Of course, it wasn't completely demolished. It wasn't total damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What had happened to the Levi's? You'd packed up all the Levi's to deliver to Travnik. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was stolen. That was taken away, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there any other goods that you'd had for Travnik that you had at the house and went missing?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was some underwear and those sneakers. Some of it was prepared for that particular buyer, and another part was singled out for our retail outlets, within our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Kupreskic, had you, in fact, stored that stuff? Prior to taking it to Travnik, you had put it somewhere in the house. Where had you put it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, first, we unloaded it in the garage, Ivica and I, and then, since we had to separate those two lots, some of it had to stay with the company and another one packed for that buyer, then my wife and I took it upstairs, and those labels or, rather, some stickers, we put them on the Levi's and made the inventory and wrote out the invoice. So that these goods were simply upstairs on the first floor of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: All right. So they were above the room where you found your father and the soldiers; yes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Those goods were on the same floor where I lived, where those soldiers were. Because I was planning not to waste any time that morning, I mean, to take all those goods as soon as I got up and to take it, because there weren't too many goods there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You were, in fact, sent away from the house by the soldier. You've described that event. One of the soldiers told you to scram and come back later. When you went back for your father, you say that the soldiers had gone; yes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You stated that you were able to take some food from the refrigerator, so presumably they hadn't stolen the food; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is. They did not. But from my father's refrigerator downstairs, I took it from below because I found it in his refrigerator. When I was upstairs at 1.00, there was nothing. Everything was upside down. Everything was destroyed. On the round table there, I saw that they had taken my food from my refrigerator, even from the larder, and eating there and sticking their knives into the table. It was a tragic scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, check the entire house at that time, when you got back to the house on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Come on, no. I only entered the front door, to the first floor, and to those two rooms. While I was there, I could only see those two rooms and not in full yet and, of course, the passage and the staircase, and that was all that I could see that day. I even dared not -- in the evening, around 6.00, and even then, I dare not go round and inspect the place because I was expecting them to come any time again, and I realised what it was all about. I realised that it was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Clearly we cannot say as to whether the damage or whatever has happened to your home was due to the events of the 16th of April or, indeed, may have been on subsequent days as the war unfolded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This destruction took place on the 16th, and I assume that it went on on the 17th. I said they would not allow me to approach the house even. I think they destroyed it slowly, those military men, and also the Muslim houses on the 17th and 18th, and that is what I heard later on from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've also heard, have you not, in this court, I believe, one of the British military made a statement that on the day he saw your house, amongst others, and like most of the Croat-owned houses, it appeared to be undamaged, by comparison certainly to those of the Muslim neighbours whose houses had been destroyed. What do you have to say to that, sir? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that man never said here that he had seen me that day, nor could he see me on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm referring, sir, to your house, that those houses had been seen by him that day and they were not damaged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That day -- what he saw that day, I really cannot say. But that day, yes, of course, my house was not as destroyed as, very likely, the houses of my neighbours were. Because only for a moment when that soldier took me out, I saw Sukrija Ahmic's house, that is, my neighbour's house, on fire, and, of course, it was in a worse condition than my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have one last point to put to you, sir, regarding the question of the house, and that is this: Is it correct that the document you produced, I believe, to this Court was created in 1995? Because that's the time that the claim was put in and the claim was formulated. It was in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, it was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have reached a contextual complete break point here to move on to other matters. There are essentially two major documents I propose to refer to after the luncheon break, if you care to take it now. One is the war diary that is already before the Chamber. There is the interview that was conducted by my learned friend, Mr. Terrier, with the accused back in 1998. Perhaps I can just tender that to you before lunch so that, administratively, we have it ready --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: -- and then I will have little by way of documentary references and things after that, and I won't be taking very long either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. May I take this opportunity to ask Counsel Krajina whether he would like to tender into evidence the sketch made by Vlatko Kupreskic, the sketch the witness used this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why not? I thought it would be useful. Anyway, if you don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: In that case, thank you very much, and in that case, we are tendering it into evidence as a Defence Exhibit. We simply thought that it was his own private sketch. We didn't know about it beforehand. But thank you very much for this suggestion, and, yes, we do tender it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. President, I won't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. It is admitted into evidence. We will adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is one exhibit that has to be tendered into evidence. It is the sketch made by Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be D62/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, one question remains I would like to clear up regarding the time that you went to the house for the first time to see your father. Can you tell me, please, how long you stayed at the house where your father and the soldiers were both present?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot be very specific. I believe that I did not stay for more than 15 to 20 minutes, considering all things that went on there. Even today, it seems to me as if this was a much longer period of time, but perhaps it was, all in all, about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I wonder if Defence Exhibit 13/1 could be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Kupreskic, I would like really to clear up something I could have covered earlier, but I believe that the photographs you are now looking at represent the shelter accommodation at the Vrebac house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, whereabouts in that shelter you went when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We went down the stairs to the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you tell us which picture number you're going to refer to?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were here (indicating), to the left as you come down the stairs, in this room to the left which you cannot see here in the picture, because not all rooms are shown in the photographs. But I remember that these two rooms were on the other side, the opposite side. They did not have any doors, so there were just like openings. Where we were, that room did have a door. So you cannot see it. It's picture number 4, but you cannot see the room itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it possible that we can just see the edge of the door frame on the left side of that picture? Is that the doorway you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, here you can just barely see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Did you remain in that room for the whole time you stayed at the shelter?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, because I was one of the last ones to arrive in the shelter, and there were already quite a few people there, especially the rooms downstairs. So fairly shortly thereafter, I climbed back upstairs. It's -- let's say in photograph number 1, I went into this hallway here (indicating). When you enter here, there is a hallway, and there are two or three additional rooms here on this level. I also remember I also used a toilet here, and you can see the window here (indicating). And then you can also see the windows to the rooms. I remember that the parquet floor became twisted a little bit, because nobody lived there, and it was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kupreskic. Now, sir, moving on, I'm going to ask you some questions relating to any time up to and including the 16th of April, 1993, but no further at this point. Have you, sir, up to and including the 16th of April, 1993, ever owned a firearm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Until 16 April, 1993, if that is the date that you were referring to, I never had a rifle. I said that I acquired the rifle only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. Did you have any other form of firearm -- maybe a pistol, or anything of that nature -- in your possession up to the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I believe -- in fact, I did acquire, in a legal way, a pistol. I don't know exactly when. I think it was perhaps as early as 1985, because I travelled a lot, I moved around a lot, even at night, in different areas. So I got a regular permit, and I acquired a pistol. But believe it or not, in all those ten years, I perhaps fired up to ten rounds from that weapon, and perhaps it was also -- my father may have used it for celebrations, because we have a custom to shoot in the air during celebrations sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You said you bought it because you travelled a lot and so forth; does that mean that you used, in fact, to carry the pistol with you for self-protection?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I usually kept it in the car, in the glove compartment, for personal protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I am presuming, Mr. Kupreskic, that the ten rounds you fired were just a bit of practice with the weapon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I was never interested in weapons. I only -- I don't even know myself, because once at home, while I was showing a friend this pistol, it accidentally fired, and I nearly killed myself and my friend. From then on, I did not carry it around at all. So we can take it to an expert; you will see. They will be able to tell you no more than ten bullets were ever fired from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So again I would ask: Were those bullets fired in a kind of target-practice way, those ten bullets? Or what were the circumstances they were fired in?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The circumstances under which it fired, I didn't even know how it was locked or not, but my father would use it -- let's say for Christmas, he would shoot from it as some celebration. But I never practised or I never used it. I wasn't interested in that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The occasion you had an accidental discharge of the weapon, can you tell us, please, when did that happen? In fact, sir, what year was that in?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was in 1988, 1989. I cannot recall exactly, but around that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But as regards any other kind of weapon -- and by that I mean a rifle or, you know, a hunting weapon, a long-barrelled weapon -- you say you've never had one up to and including April 1993? That's correct, sir? Yes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct. I never had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you at any time over that same time period ever have occasion to have such a weapon in your possession just temporarily, lodged with you by a friend, or in some other way in your possession for a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I only recall one episode which was even funny. On the 16th of April, when I came back from the house around 1.00 p.m., I said that -- when I came out of the larger forest and near the smaller forest, I saw Drago Grgic, and he was carrying a small rifle. I later learned that it belonged to Ivica Kupreskic. But it's a small hunting carbine. It was a trophy weapon. So Ivica had gave it to him for safekeeping, and he told me, "Here is a rifle and give it to Ivica." I didn't know what kind of weapon it was, where it came from. As he was giving it to me, the rifle discharged, and then immediately, I said, "I don't want it." I thought that I'd kill myself and others. Anto Vidovic, called Satko, was there, so he can confirm that. So this rifle was in my possession for several seconds, and I only later learned that Ivica actually owned that rifle and that he later got it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I will now turn, if I may, to your document, the war diary. Could you perhaps pick that up? I think it's next to you, Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I just want to refer to a few entries in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first one I'm going to look at is page 2 of the war diary and the entry for the 8th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With your permission, Mr. Prosecutor, I would like to clarify for the Chamber this diary so that everybody would be able to more easily follow these entries to see what they are. This diary has a total of 49 pages. The first 12 pages, including the blank page, the first 12 pages refer to the notes and information of my activity in the SPS company for the period of 1987 and 1988 when I was in a commission for housing. So the first 12 pages refer to 1987 and 1988, and they are my notes covering my activities at the company. The next 15 pages, and I marked them 1 through 15, they are a war journal or war diary. So that would cover the pages starting at page 13, where every day, I entered what I did. So that is the period when I was mobilised as a driver, as an ambulance driver, 15 September, 1993 until 27 April, 1994 when I was demobilised, in other words, when I was released from this duty. So those 15 pages cover this war diary, as I call it. Then the following 22 pages, starting at page 27 to page 49, all those 22 pages refer to my preparation of my defence before this Trial Chamber and notes which I took in 1996 and 1997. So now this is probably clear, that we can divide it into these three areas. So one is from the SPS company, the second segment is the wartime activities, and the third is my preparation for my defence before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I can refer to the second section, Mr. Kupreskic, I would ask you to look now, in fact, at the entry, this will shorten matters, for the 13th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's the bottom of page 2 in our translation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Kupreskic, that it is a correct entry by you that Dr. Bosko informed you that evening that "Bertovic had, with his support, proposed me as commander of the medical section, 1st Battalion." Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is in the top right corner, and that is 9 December, 1993. Bosko, the doctor, informed me that evening -- yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it true that if we just look at the pages after that --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With your permission, I did not fully answer the question. This is what I thought was written here, but what is this? At that time, Dr. Bosko, because I was the only male person in the medical unit, and since these infirmaries were established in there, I think there were five or six of them in that area, and knowing of my organisational skills, he asked me to help him with the control of all these infirmaries in the area of Zume where I worked as a driver. So he proposed this, and he also proposed it to Mr. Bertovic, but I declined to accept it, and you could see it from the next entries, in the same diary, on the same page, if you can follow me, in the bottom right, the entry of 17 December, 1993, where I say that I declined to accept it and that I went to complain to Mr. Sajevic and told him that I did not want to take on that job. So I talked with him on 17 December, 1993. However, as I kept my entries on a daily basis, later on, after that conversation with Mr. Sajevic, I received an oral order, and I had no way out. So I just assisted Dr. Bosko, and I never received any document or a written appointment to that duty. Now, what this duty was, if I was going to go around and to -- for me to go around and visit all these different infirmaries, but I never received any document about it. You will see later on, I think this was on the 20th of December, that I was ordered to help Dr. Bosko and go on visiting all these other infirmaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, Mr. Kupreskic, that, as I say, looking at these various pages, we see, as you say, many visits to clinics and outpatient departments as part of your duties. If I may turn your attention now, it will be page 8, Your Honours, for ourselves, to the entries from the 1st of February, 1994 to the 4th of February, 1994, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. These are not clinics really. These are just village outpatient facilities. There were not even any professional medical staff. I am not a doctor to go around and visit clinics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What I want to ask you about these entries, if I may, in the beginning of February, there are references to inspection of soldiers, and particularly the 3rd of February, 1994, "inspection carried out at," and then the 4th of February, "inspection again, and again response weak." Were these inspections, in some way, carried out by you on behalf of Dr. Bosko, or were they carried out by other people? Can you tell me what they involved, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In brief, since I was ordered to assist Dr. Bosko, and we did not have and still to date we do not have a doctor there, so what I did is I just kept notes or records of what the commission would establish or diagnose, after having examined these people. So I was just a note or a record taker there. In a way, I still did the type of work that I was able to do. And I'm not an expert to establish the disabilities of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, let's say this: You've explained, for instance, the document from the police administration where, in order to pay you, they called you by a title, investigator, inspector, whatever. Is it, therefore, logical that when the certificate was issued by the HVO regarding your supposed service periods, the description of "performing the duties of assistant commander for health matters," would that have been a convenient way to describe the way that you were the assistant to Dr. Bosko?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Under no circumstances could I have been the assistant to Dr. Bosko. I know nothing about medicine, and I never performed such a duty, nor did I receive a document to that effect. This document presented by the Prosecutor is something that I saw for the first time here, and I find it highly suspicious, when it was written, how, and what its source is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could we have Prosecution Exhibit 329, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, this we have on the machine at the moment -- you have the Bosnian language one in front of you, the Croatian one in front of you -- you say that that document you never saw in your life until produced in court by the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. I saw it for the first time here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, do you recall a briefcase being taken from you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do remember my briefcase, but I don't know when it was seized. I just learnt later that it had been taken from my house. But I do not remember ever seeing such a document, nor of it being in that briefcase. I never saw it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, may I put it to you that when the contents of that briefcase were inventoried by the Office of the Prosecutor, that document was found in your briefcase. Now, you still say that you have no knowledge of that document?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do claim that. Let me tell you something. I received a document with the address and telephone of Anto Furundzija's mother, which shows that this is some sort of speculation, I don't know on whose part. But I never knew Anto Furundzija, I met him here in the detention centre, not to mention his mother and her telephone number. Where did that come from? Where did the name of his mother appear, and her telephone number? And the same can be said of this certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, the HVO booklet, military booklet describing you as unfit, that was found in your briefcase. Do you agree that that was there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My military booklet was there in my briefcase, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it also true, sir, that there was a tape recorder with a cassette tape in it that was also in your briefcase?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, all that is correct, with the exception of these two documents. This one, which I really don't remember, I never saw it before, except in here, and the address and telephone number of Furundzija's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You also had such items as a passport, you had business documents, and you had a number of other personal papers in that briefcase, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All that is true, but allow me to say that those things and documents travelled. You know that yourself; we had a discussion about that here. And that briefcase was opened, and it travelled from one place to another, so anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Isn't it somewhat remarkable, Mr. Kupreskic, that this document contains your name, your father's name, your date and place of birth, the fact that you were in the medical service in the 92nd Viteska Home Guard Regiment, you certainly were involved in the medical side of work, and that you were demobilised on the 15th of January, 1996? Now, isn't it a bit unbelievable that all that information on a document could have somehow found its way into your briefcase without your knowledge? Wouldn't you be aware of having such a document? I suggest, sir, you were aware of it, and it was in your possession, and you know it was in your briefcase, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These data here are not correct, except for my personal data, my name and where and when I was born. The dates, time, it is absolutely not correct. You saw here, on the 13th page of my diary, which I couldn't have made up, that I was demobilised on the 15th of September, 1993, as an ambulance driver, and that I performed that duty, I think, until the 27th of April, 1993. And all that is clearly written in my diary. I couldn't have made that up. This was seized from me unexpectedly, wasn't it? So the date is absolutely not correct, nor is the name of the function I performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But the question --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: And you see, also, the date of the 15th of January, 1958 -- rather, that it says I was demobilised on the 15th of January, 1996. I had been working by then for two years in the Sutre firm and later on in my own firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you are disputing that that document was ever present in your briefcase; is that right, sir? Despite the fact that we have an affidavit to say that it was taken from your briefcase. I'll leave it at that. If I can return to your war diary document for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would add that I have very few questions left, Your Honours; I shall be concluding shortly. Page 17 on our translation, Your Honours, if you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you look at the entry that is on the 8th of August, 1996? It's just towards the end of your entry for that date, just before the 9th of August, 1996.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've found the page. The 8th of August, 1996. It says "Thursday."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you see, written by you, towards the end of that entry, the name Zvonimir Hodak?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please help me to find it? I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, in our translation, we have the 9th of August, 1996, listed as a date. Would you look just above the 9th of August, 1996?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't seem to able to find that date. Yes, I see it now, on your copy. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You make a list of clothing there, sir. What -- in what context? You talk about a chocolate-coloured suede coat with fur lining, olive-coloured corduroy trousers. What is that list about?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am saying this because I was preparing my defence, and this was in my diary. I wrote down what I was wearing on that morning, the 16th of April, 1993, in civilian clothes, and I am describing with precision, and where I say in the fifth paragraph, as for armaments, I had nothing. After the clothing, then the dash, fifth dashes down, it says of arms, I had none. I had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doesn't it also say, "But on the way back I was given a small-calibre rifle belonging to I.K. and three or four bullets," which I presume is the incident you've just described to us?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, for a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I turn attention now to the interview document of the Prosecutor's interview. That's in the document we submitted. It's a record of interview with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and that document has been handed in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 381.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will not go over ground that has been covered, I'm sure quite exhaustively, in many areas, but, Mr. Kupreskic, is it correct that you told the representatives of the OTP -- namely Mr. Terrier and Mr. Smith -- when you were interviewed that when you were called and you went to see your father before going to the shelter, your father actually said to you "'You, yourself, know we never had any problems,' so he remained in the house and others left to the shelter"? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Probably I did, because indeed, it may have been like that. I can't now remember all the details, but we really never did have any problems from anyone. And at the time, I repeat again, and I underline in this interview, that those details, at the time, I thought were not important, whereas today and now, I have a different opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You said, and it is recorded on the English translation at page 14, second large paragraph down, you said, "At 9.00 a.m. I was in the shelter, they told us that we can come out of the shelter into the yard of the shelter, when I came out my wife and children remained in the shelter. I was shocked by what I saw, I said: "My God, this is real war." And then you said, "No shooting there, there was no shooting in the vicinity anymore, but the houses were on fire already, especially the houses near my house." You then express concern because your father was still at home and then offered to draw a sketch of the location of your home. Mr. Kupreskic, you said then that at 9.00 a.m. you were actually outside the shelter, and there was no shooting. The question then is, why didn't you go to your father then, if that is correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please show me the page? Tell me the page where I can find this. Page 13, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, I'm working from an English translation, Mr. Kupreskic, so we possibly have a problem to marry them up. But the question -- I'll try and get a way to orientate you. I'm told it's around page 13, and you had just been asked --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If you would just read on a couple of paragraphs, sir, that's the bit I mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's my question: Is that accurate? Was it in fact quiet at 9.00? Were you outside the shelter? And if so, why didn't you go up to your house then?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You see, it says quite clearly here, after the initials "V.K.," my name, I was in the shelter until 9.30, but it is not properly written. I think everything coincides with what I testified yesterday. I said that about 9.30, I went out. I left the shelter and went to a hill outside, because the shooting seemed to have subsided. From there, I could see the smoke, and there was still some shooting, and then I said, "God, it really is a war." I think that in my statement I also described the situation similarly, but the discussion about such details, on the basis of which we later broke off this interview, in those days I wasn't focused on such details, as I have been now, during these two days of my testimony. At the time, I didn't think that it was so important for me to describe everything. That interview wasn't conceived in that way. We had sought, as we had agreed, and you know that a year previously, I presented my defence to the Prosecution, and one of the reasons, the most important reason that I asked to testify, was to clarify for Their Honours these details that we are talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, with all due respect, at that time, you were held in detention in a prison. You were being questioned by representatives of the Prosecution. You were in the presence of two defence attorneys, Mr. Krajina and Mr. Par, and yet you say you conducted yourself on the basis that you didn't think the details were that important? Is that what you're trying to say to us, sir? If that's what you are saying, I accept what you say.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
