utterances.text: Yes. At the time, I thought it was not important. It even says here, I can find it for you, when I addressed Mr. Terrier and said to him, "Don't misuse my words sometime in the future." You must understand that this is my first experience in my whole life of this kind. So one of the main reasons, and you saw that I was the first to ask to testify in court in order to explain everything to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, towards the bottom of what is page 15 in our translation, it may be probably another eight paragraphs on from where you are now, you referred to how you became involved in the work in the medical service, and one little sentence in there is this: "I could not refuse this, since even until that time, I always received negative criticism because of my passivity." So, in fact, did you exhibit willingness to assist the HVO in that respect, in that work, in order to change a possible perception of yourself as not willing to partake? Is that what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I avoided any commitment. Which normal man would want to go to war and to perform duties in wartime? I think I am a normal man, and I never wanted to accept that. However, when the army threatens you and when they give you orders, you had no choice. Is it a crime that I helped people during the war in the town of Vitez? I helped wounded Muslims as well. I have a witness who made a statement here, she's a Muslim, and I helped her with my own car. She made a statement, and she certified that statement in the municipality. She's a Muslim witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just one final thing. You indicated, when interviewed, that you signed a number of commercial documents when you were in Split. Did you retain possession of those documents to prove the transactions you entered into?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not what I said. If you are referring to the 14th of April, 1993, we had only one contact and agreement in the company Koteks. Before that, all I can say is that we had agreements and contracts, and we have the necessary documents also in the company Uzor in Split, which engaged in textile trade, and Jugoplastika and Brodomerkur companies. These are all major companies with which we cooperated, and I think there is my business notebook still somewhere, like this diary, from which I can show you the business contacts that we had with those enterprises in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, you also made reference in that interview to the house, that when you went back to the house to see your father, and you were asked -- Your Honours, this is page 32 of the interview document -- "What kind of damage to your house did you see?" And you gave a description which I suggest was -- you said, "The front door was broken into, the lock of the second door shot off. All the windows were open overlooking the road to Ahmici. The bedroom was destroyed," and then you discovered what you've already stated here today and yesterday, about mud and soil, probably from dirty boots. Do you maintain today that that is still an accurate description of the damage to the property?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course it is accurate. What I said then and all that I have said in these past two days, I think I described everything well. I mention here that especially when I arrived with my wife, some ten days later, when I reached my house, then we saw in detail what had happened, and I think that all these things fully coincide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to move on to another topic. It's brief. I have a small amount of audiotape to play. It is just a few moments, a few lines of conversation. I would be grateful if that could be played at this moment. Yes, we do have transcripts for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We also need a number for the interview. Exhibit 381, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The tape will be Prosecution Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, allow me. We don't know what this is, what kind of tape, what document is going to be shown. It has not been disclosed to us, so I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, you heard reference by myself a little earlier to Mr. Kupreskic regarding the contents of his briefcase which included a tape recorder and a piece of audiotape, a cassette. It is the audio cassette that was recovered from his briefcase, and in respect of that, a receipt was duly signed by my learned friend Mr. Krajina as the fact that that was being retained by the Office of the Prosecutor, when the other items or possessions, including the briefcase, were returned to Mr. Kupreskic. That is the source of that tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Have you so far disclosed this tape to Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It was my understanding that that is so, and, indeed, it was referred to -- it was, in fact, included in a formal pleading entered on the 20th of May, 1998 when the Prosecutor's report on chain of custody of Vlatko Kupreskic's briefcase was filed. In fact, in the final paragraph of that, at paragraph 14, it states: "Briefcase shows that none of the items claimed by Mr. Kupreskic to be missing from his bag were, in fact, in the briefcase when received by ICTY," et cetera, and the preceding paragraph 13 states: "Originals or copies of all items found in the Kupreskic briefcase, with the exception only of a cassette tape recorder, were returned with the briefcase." So it is my understanding that certainly there should have been a copy returned to Mr. Krajina at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm really surprised by this. We never saw nor were we given that cassette. Without offending anyone, I think it is inaccurate, and I don't know why such a method is being applied. Probably intentionally we were not given that cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: This relates to issues dating back to the 4th of February, 1998, Your Honours. I would like to have a brief word with my colleagues. Obviously, I wasn't on the case at that time. I would like to check a point. Your Honours, my colleague and I, we did, in fact, meet with Mr. Par and Mr. Krajina out of court yesterday, and I am certain in my own mind that this was mentioned and that the problem we had was at the time a formal translation of the tape wasn't ready, but we had a draft translation and that that was in their hands. So I'm a little taken aback that my learned friend should clearly have had some misunderstanding with ourselves as to what this document was, because we referred to it as the tape we were going to play. We certainly, as I say, said there could have been a problem over the translation. Now, if this was a communication problem between us, then that is unfortunate and regrettable, but, as I say, I can rely only on the file pleading dating back to the 20th of May of last year and apparently that everybody was aware from that time that the Prosecution were retaining the tape and recorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But, again, you are speaking of the transcript. What about the tape, as such? Did you hand over the tape to Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That, I am trying to verify as to whether, in fact, a copy of the tape itself was handed over. I'm advised that is so, that a copy of the tape was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I find this offensive. No tape has ever been handed over to me and my assistants. Never. I should like to ask my learned friend to really be more careful, to pick his words more carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have filed information before me, Your Honours. All I can do is quote to you from that: "There had been complaint at that time by Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic regarding the non-return of certain items he alleged were in the briefcase." The war diary was mentioned. Well, it was indicated that a copy would be provided, and it was, and the original was retained. There was an entry for the tape recorder stating: "Vlatko also complained his tape recorder was not returned. It was explained it was being kept for evidentiary purposes and that a copy of the tape has been provided to him." Now, that's the information I had from the file. I can say no more than that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we have a witness here, he's very near here, Mr. McFaden, the warden, he, because I wouldn't have it otherwise, he took it over in the presence of witnesses, it was all in writing and with a signature, all the documents that the Prosecutor gave me back, and that tape was never given to me. You can call Mr. McFaden, and there is his signature because he was a member of that commission. So that is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We feel that since there are doubts about whether or not this tape was handed over to Counsel Krajina, we will not allow it. I have no reason to doubt what Counsel Krajina said. Probably there was a misunderstanding. It happens. There was a mistake and it was not handed over to Counsel Krajina, so we can't allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We will certainly check the position, of course, Your Honours. I can understand your qualms. Perhaps Your Honours might permit me to ask one or two questions relating to the existence of this. It may then be something that if properly provable to your satisfaction, it could, in fact, be dealt with briefly on rebuttal when the time comes. I don't know if that possibly could be the case, but perhaps if I can just reserve the position in that way, I could ask a couple of brief questions and leave it at that for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, you do recall that in your briefcase, there was a tape recorder; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did that tape recorder contain a cassette cape or was there a cassette tape in the briefcase?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you be prepared to say what that tape contained? Was it conversation? Was it music? What did it contain?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I will. I'll tell you all. Well, you know that I and my defence never left any question open until this very last moment, so I shall be very happy to answer because there is nothing suspicious about that, and Their Honours should also know it. It was a small cassette in my dictaphone, which is a Philips make, and I tried to record on it that soldier whom I met as I was going back from my house at 13.00, because I thought that he looked like that man and I thought it was that man. As he remembered when Drago Grgic -- and Drago Grgic was killed and he is not alive -- and perhaps he might remember when Drago Grgic was giving me that rifle which went off. When I announced for a position for a driver in my company, a fellow from Zenica applied, and he looked to me like this soldier whom I met on the 16th of April, 1993, around 13.00, whom I found there together with Drago Grgic and Anto Vidovic, nicknamed Satko. So as I was preparing my defence before this Court, I made a recording of that, and I asked him, "Do you remember that and would you confirm it tomorrow, if that is you, if that is what you looked like," that man, "and would you be my witness?" You can find it also in my diary. Not to waste more time, I mean, that is what it says in the diary. I'm not going to look for the page now, but it says that that soldier who was there and saw that scene, and I even say there how we laughed about it because I really haven't a clue about weapons. I thought that it was important and I wanted him to corroborate this important thing. So that's what this audio cassette was about. I don't think there's any problem, and we don't mind hearing it because that is what this tape says word for word. I do not think there is anything that might give rise to any doubts or anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kupreskic. However, Counsel Krajina objected to the production of this audiotape. Therefore, for the time being, we will not allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know that once you have ruled, you have ruled, but I do, in fact, have a copy of a letter sent the 24th of February, 1998 to both Mr. Krajina and Mr. Par --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going too fast. In fact, it refers to a Philips tape recorder with one tape, and it says, "However, a copy of the tape located inside was returned to your client." I am advised that that was advised in writing to Mr. Krajina on the 24th of February, 1998 and apparently returned to his client. But I know it's causing him qualms and problems. Maybe, with your leave, we could preserve the issue for rebuttal and make sure that everybody is happy at that time. It won't take more than a few minutes out of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the matter has been resolved. But I merely want to say that this statement, from that document that my learned friend mentions, is what we disputed. Hence, all the correspondence and discussion here in court because we were affirming that these things were not returned to us, as this document seems to purport. That is not true. You must remember the decisions of the Chamber to verify, to check it, to go into the matter and resolve it, but it was never fully clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think the position is resolved, Your Honours, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have just a couple more brief areas, Mr. Kupreskic. We shall be just a very few minutes. Is it true that in 1995 you purchased a weapon at the suggestion of your wife?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not purchase a weapon at my wife's proposal. I was given a rifle in 1995. I believe it was January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We have seen a weapon that I would call a Kalashnikov-type automatic actually shown to your wife earlier in these proceedings, and, of course, you were present at that time. Is that the gun, Mr. Kupreskic? Is that the gun that you had, the one that was shown to your wife when she came here to testify?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I guess so. I don't dispute that. I don't know the number or what it looked like. When I brought it in January 1995, I put it there, I never touched it, I never moved it, I never took it up, so I don't think it really would serve any purpose and it would be a waste of time if you showed it to me. I don't dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon me for wasting the time to do so, Mr. Kupreskic, but I would like you to look at that weapon. Does that remind you --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's a rifle similar to the one that I obtained in 1995. It's similar, but it's a rifle. A rifle is a rifle is a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mention has been made of the time when you were actually arrested by SFOR troops, and you stated, I believe, that you thought there were burglars in the house, you took up the weapon --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist the usher. I can see no further use of the weapon being produced in court. Perhaps you can take it back. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say you thought there were burglars in the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sure. When I heard those shots, the noise, first, I dreamed and I said, "Oh, it's war again," but then I woke up, and I thought it was thieves, because our house has been attacked before that in 1994, 1995, twice in 1994, and in 1997 too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say your house had been attacked. In what way had your house been attacked over those years? Was that attacked by military people or do you mean burglars broke into it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, those were burglars. They were thieves. You must understand, I have a company, and they must have thought I had money there, and they burgled the house, they broke into the house while I was away, when I was on a business trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I recall you saying in your evidence in chief, Mr. Kupreskic, that you heard detonations at the time of the people, you say, breaking into your house, which is when you were arrested; is that right? You heard detonations?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I told you, at first, I thought I was dreaming because those detonations were like those that I experienced on the 16th of April. There was gunfire, it was thundering, it was dim all around, and I don't really know. I mean, all that happened defies common sense, because I'm telling you, I mean, there was no need for all that. First the bombs were thrown in, and my wife knows better about this, because bombs were -- I mean, grenades were thrown in to the ground floor at my mother's where she sleeps in her bedroom. Thanks be to God that my mother was in Germany visiting with her sister, and that's why she survived. But would you believe that on the 17th of December I was with them twice, and I never hid, and it all looked like a circus. But let me, Your Honours, let me just tell you this whole story. Seven days later -- no, no, no; allow me, Mr. Prosecutor. Major Kusuk (phoen) visited my family with an interpreter who was a Muslim, and I don't know if there was another member yet. They came to my house. I was in the hospital then, and my family, my wife admitted them as due, offered them drinks, and even prepared some meats for them. And he left with my family, with my wife, this calling card -- and this is the original; I can show it to you -- and said, when he saw my body and me in Novi Travnik, when he saw the documentation and what men it was all about, he apologised to my family, and that is the only satisfaction that I have received in this case so far. So this is his calling card, that major's, and I am most grateful to him. It was a nice gesture. And of course, everybody can be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, I would like to put one factual suggestion to you for your comment, briefly, I hope. The arresting troops indicated that two bursts of fire from an automatic weapon came from you towards them prior to your, in fact, being wounded and secured as a prisoner. Is it true that you fired two small bursts at the people concerned?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it is not true. I didn't know how to let off bursts of fire. I managed somehow to aim, and I believe I fired two bullets into the ceiling, because my wife told me that later; she was watching it from about a two-, three-metre distance. Because I didn't know how to fire, and when the first bullet came out, I was scared stiff, because -- I mean, this rifle jumped in my hands, and I didn't know what it was. It all took two or three seconds, and I simply threw away that rifle. I then lost consciousness, and those people did, yes, take me to a couch, and then I asked if anybody was wounded, but nobody was even scratched or wounded. I have never in my life had a rifle, nor did I know what a rifle was, but I thought they were burglars. I merely said, "Why did you do this to me? There was no need for it."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Kupreskic. Just one last point, if I may cover it with you. In the past, you indicated your family had had some difficulty, several people had had difficulty over boundaries with Mr. Sakib Ahmic. He apparently was a hard man to live with about respecting boundaries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My family had no problems with him, and particularly I. I mean, I had no trouble with him. But we had known one another for about 30 years. My father and he lived together. He did cause small problems, small trouble, not only to my father but his Muslim neighbours. He was simply a rather ill-tempered man. But I didn't have any particular problem with him. I wasn't interested in land. I was interested in much more intelligent things than land.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, in front of your house these days there is an area which, in fact, on the aerial photograph, appears white. Is it true that after your return to Ahmici, some raised ground or some hill that was in front of your property was scraped level and the earth removed? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That hill, I can show it, was right next to my shop's door (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Correct. Where did you place the earth that was scraped off that surface? Could you tell me where you tipped it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a moment. I took it in front of the warehouse, in front of my shop. But that is not my plot of land. That plot belongs to my neighbours, Latif and Atif Ahmic. They were grateful to me because I levelled off that elevation, that hill, and now they've got better soil there, and they're grateful to me. You can go to them and ask them if I'm telling the truth, because I paid a couple of thousand marks for that. To this day, I use their plot of land as a parking lot, and they never said anything. They are grateful to me. Recently they came, my wife told me, and they themselves took away, without ever being asked, they removed the garbage that was in front of my shop, but of course did not charge a dinar for it, a penny for it. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (redacted), because I also levelled part of his plot of land, and he also was grateful for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can I ask you just one thing, because it was raised by that witness: Was there any encroachment of the boundaries of the ground of (redacted) as a result of the work you did in front of your premises? You can answer that as just "Yes" or "No," sir.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't answer it like that. I mean, part of some earth, because there was plenty of earth, some of it was taken to (redacted) lot. But I again have witnesses, the machine came. When he complained, all the earth was removed there, everything was cleared up, and there was no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. I am obliged for your indulgence. I would like, please, to tender exhibits which have been marked P377, 378, 379, 380, and 381.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we decide on when to take a break, Counsel Krajina, may I ask you whether you intend to re-examine the witness for long?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Only one, only one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us then proceed right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, at the end of your testimony, I shall ask you only this: Would you like to say something that nobody asked you during this, your testimony here? Is there anything that you should like to clear up? Is there any statement you should like to make with regard to the charges brought against you and the evidence adduced so far in this case?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I should only like to add that I'm grateful to you, Mr. President, I'm grateful to Your Honours for listening to me carefully, and I believe I succeeded in showing what I have been claiming from the first day, and that is that I am not guilty and that no charge against me holds water. You will remember that the first time that I was allowed to speak, I said that for the things that I'm being charged for, I never had either the opportunity or the possibility or courage or interest to commit, and I also said that my Muslim neighbours would corroborate that, and I have proven it. My defence counsel and I never had any open question or any dispute with the gentlemen from the Prosecution. You know that my defence and my documents, and all my documents, I disclosed more than a year ago; that I was never afraid of the truth. Yet another reason why I did not come with my colleagues is perhaps the fact that it will shortly be two years, that more than two years would elapse before my case is finally closed. My colleagues and I have been suffering for three years because of this case. So Mr. President, Your Honours, I should like to ask you to help me, to instruct me, to tell me, what else do I and my defence counsel need to do to show that I am not guilty? I know that the gentlemen from the Prosecution were very correct and performed their job duly, but please, what else do I have to do to show you that I am not guilty? I cannot really tell you all, but go to Ahmici whenever you like, and you will see, both in the shop and in my house, in my home, you will see Muslim neighbours. Believe it or not, Witness L, the one who accused me here, he sent me his greetings through my daughter and inquired after my health. Witness Q passes by my house every day. True, he bows his head because he is ashamed. But another witness who was announced by the Prosecution today, a Muslim, an Ahmic, passes by my house every day and stops there, pauses there. So what else is in dispute here? I'm bound to say that I am sorry about what befell my Muslim neighbours, and that I condemn it very strongly. But Your Honours, please try to understand me and my family. I'm the only male in that family. I'm a father, I'm their only provider, and yet I'm a sick man, and I wonder, how did I manage to survive this year and a half in detention? It's only after a year and so many months I have been given the first opportunity to explain to Your Honours that I am not guilty of what I'm being charged with. My defence will submit the motion, request for my provisional release, and will do it this afternoon or tomorrow morning. I do hope that you will meet that request, and I do beg you, if our families are unhappy, if my Muslim neighbours -- and they're all innocent -- my Muslim neighbours' families are suffering and they are innocent, why should my family also suffer because they are innocent too. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have no questions for you, Mr. Kupreskic. Thank you very much indeed for giving evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any outstanding matter? I wonder whether, before we adjourn, whether -- I see -- Counsel Susak, are you going to -- no? Anybody wishing to raise any issue before -- Counsel Susak, yes, I thought I had seen you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, due to the briefness of time, I did not submit a motion for the provisional release of Drago Josipovic, so if I may, I should like to take advantage of this moment to do so, because we are leaving for Zagreb tomorrow. I will be very brief, as I have prepared it. It is my view that exceptional circumstances do exist which justify a decision by the Trial Chamber on the provisional release of Drago Josipovic. An exceptional circumstance is the death of his mother, who died on the 6th of May this year. She took care of Drago Josipovic's children, and especially Nikola, born in 1984, who is going to first grade of secondary school, because the mother of the children, Slavica Josipovic, is too busy. She is the only one in the family to make a livelihood for the upkeep and education of her children, so she doesn't have sufficient time to devote herself to the children. The older son, Goran, was born in 1979, and he is on the first year of studies of transport science in Zagreb. In view of what has been said, the children are lacking the necessary control and supervision, which can have negative effects on their upbringing and education. They were emotionally linked to their father, and by his provisional release, this would be of the greatest assistance to his children, Nikola and Goran. They find it very difficult to cope with their father's absence. Another exceptional circumstance in this particular case is that all the witnesses have been heard in court of both the Prosecution and the Defence with respect to the defence of Drago Josipovic. Furthermore, the additional witnesses envisaged by the Prosecutor do not relate to the defence of Drago Josipovic. The trial has been going on for a long time, and as is known, the Trial Chamber has already previously taken a decision on his provisional release when he was allowed to go to Santici to attend the funeral of his mother. Drago Josipovic, without any special control measures, went to Santici, stayed there, and came back to the detention unit in The Hague. Drago Josipovic voluntarily surrendered to the International Criminal Tribunal. When he learnt of the indictment, he did not change his place of residence. The Tribunal has already had occasion to see for themselves that Drago Josipovic will appear in court and that he will not represent a threat or danger to any victim or witness or any other person. We therefore propose that the Trial Chamber pass a decision whereby the request for provisional release of Drago Josipovic will be granted. This motion is based on Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That is all, and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecution would like to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very briefly. The reality, of course, very sadly, is that for anybody undergoing trial who is in a situation where liberty during that trial is denied, as is the general rule here, due to the severity and seriousness of the crimes alleged in war crimes trials, the difficulties that are sustained by relatives, children, and so forth, are a sad element that goes alongside that process. As a result, one has to, I respectfully submit, Your Honours, exercise considerable caution in viewing these family circumstances as being exceptional circumstances. I think the glaring example put forward in the very case of this particular accused, Mr. Josipovic, is to do with the fact of a family funeral, and indeed, it is conceded, obviously, that he honoured whatever he had to honour and returned to the court on the due day, and that is an exceptional grief, an exceptional circumstance, and was duly reflected in Your Honours' ruling. I think, however, that at this stage in proceedings, when we are facing the prospect that certainly in the case of Mr. Josipovic, pretty much the case is done and dusted, save in terms, perhaps, of one of the general witnesses as to the persecution count in rebuttal, the reality is that the evidence has indeed, as my learned friend Mr. Susak's point --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It has been heard, but the bottom line is that we are being asked to consider a position where, in those circumstances, essentially awaiting the next step, which is the verdict of the Tribunal, there must be an enormous pressure on any accused, particularly an accused of very serious matters, the pressure upon them not to return must, as a human factor, be very high indeed. The other factor is that I suggest that again, the reality of some family difficulties which have been present to date, of course, do not make them exceptional as of now simply because the court is going into recess for a couple of months. Taking forward from there, we do, of course, suggest that, as pointed out by my learned friend, Mr. Terrier, earlier today, in dealing with the applications made by Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac and Mr. Radovic, that the Prosecutor has a certain experience of problems with the relevant authorities within Bosnia-Herzegovina -- again, not looking at Croatia, that's a separate state, but within the twin limbs of the entity known as the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- and that, indeed, she has made certain very strong representations as regards the personage representing that state, or one limb of that, in this very country, and as a result that assurances from that quarter, which you may well seek, would not prove to be necessarily something upon which the Chamber could reasonably rely. Those, I think, are the points I would wish to make at this particular instance. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No other matter? Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, linked to this document, which I have managed to read and which we were given by the Prosecutor, that is, a person who is supposed to be the liaison officer is not performing his duties properly, I think that no guarantees can be expected from this person, and I think that in the Federation, someone else should be addressed, because I think this gentleman is not the person who could be expected to give any guarantees. We have also been informed today that this person is no longer employed here. This is the latest information. May I make one further point, since we have come to the end? Once, when we were talking about the closing argument, you said that you would like to be given a kind of summary of that closing statement which will have indications of our quotations from certain witnesses. So my question is: Do we need to prepare this summary or do we need to prepare both the summary and the entire closing statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We thought of a sort of outline, a brief outline of your closing statement, if possible, with references to the transcript to support your submissions and allegations, and then I think the bulk of our argument should be made orally. This is actually to facilitate the task of both parties. Of course, you're welcome to prepare a long brief. But I think if only for language problems, because, of course, you would write it in Croatian, so there probably would be difficulties in translating it into English. I say it's probably better and more effective to have the bulk of your statement made orally, whereas you would simply give us an outline, a sort of skeleton argument in writing. Of course, you would have one week more than the Prosecution so as to be able to respond to points made by the Prosecution. All right. I see there are no other matters. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I apologise, but a brief technical question. In connection with the witnesses that have been announced by the Prosecutor that will be called in the next stage of the proceedings, it is not quite clear to me whether the Prosecutor will give us any new statements from those witnesses. Because in our particular case, the Prosecutor has listed, as one possible witness, the court investigator who will apparently carry out some new measurements on the ground linked to the expert findings who testified in our defence case. I would like to know whether the Prosecutor will provide us with those measurements and the results of the work of that investigator for us to be able to respond, perhaps with some new counter-evidence. He has also listed another witness, whose old statement was disclosed a year or two ago, and if the Prosecutor will have a new statement from that witness, will he disclose it to us so that we should know whether we need to respond? These are things that are not quite clear to me, so I beg for an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We will certainly give you one. Our interpretation of the situation, Your Honours, is that if we have a rebuttal case, it's like a trial in miniature, and essentially Rule 66 kicks back in, that if we are going to call witnesses, we have to produce the statements, prior statements, and other materials relevant to the witness we're calling. We are certainly proceeding on that basis, and already, in fact, what we have has been served, I think, with the motion we've filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Of course, if there are further investigations by the investigator, which I understand are, indeed, in preparation, any further results will be transmitted immediately. As a result, as I say, we will approach this as if we had to go through Rule 66 all over again and see to it that, with all due speed, appropriate discovery is made in respect of anybody that we're calling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excellent. So you will give the Defence at least a few weeks before we resume?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, if there was something that delayed a piece of investigation for four weeks and we had to give two to three weeks' notice, then, regrettably, logistics may dictate it. But, in principle, it will be just as soon as anything is finished and ready, if it needs it, it will go in. Of course, one of the witnesses put forward, Mr. McLeod, the report is already in the hands of all parties, and other statements have been served. I hope I can settle any misgivings Mr. Par has. He will have anything necessary as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In particular, Counsel Par wondered about any further statement by a witness you're going to call and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think that was principally the investigator because we've referred to further investigation, and he would like to know if there is going to be further statements and stuff like that. The answer is that that is going to be a priority task, now that we are approaching our recess prior to the September hearings. Any further work in that regard, we hope to finish by -- well, to have dealt with it, at the latest, by mid to late August, depending on being able to do so even sooner. Of course, there are logistics of such a mission. But as soon as that is done, it will be served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We are now in a position to adjourn, and so we stand in recess until the 27th of September at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 4.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of September, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
